P0D00.title: Control Pilot Charging Ventilation Switch Circuit/Open
P0D00.description: Some battery types can give off gases while charging; for that case the conductive charging standards provide a state in which the vehicle asks the station for ventilation. The vehicle signals it by switching a much smaller resistor of about 270 Ω onto the pilot, which drags the level to around 3 V; the station then only delivers power where ventilation is assured. P0D00 reports that the control circuit of this ventilation switch is open. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM's Chevrolet Volt monitors the switch for plausibility only (P0D01, normalized pilot voltage 0.04-0.10 in a self-test), and CARB requires plug-in vehicles to monitor the charging system. During normal charging the switch stays open, so an open circuit often goes unnoticed except for the stored code. Shorts are P0D02/P0D03.

causes.label: Open control wire or loose connector of the ventilation switch circuit
Ventilation switch or its resistor branch open inside the module
Failed driver stage in the charging control module

symptoms: Stored code, charging usually still works
Charging system warning in the cluster

P0D01.title: Control Pilot Charging Ventilation Switch Range/Performance
P0D01.description: The ventilation switch lets the vehicle request charging state D, in which a small resistor pulls the pilot down to about 3 V and the station may only deliver power with ventilation. P0D01 means this switch does not produce a plausible pilot level. GM documents the check for the Chevrolet Volt (VICM/HPC2): in a self-test with the cord unplugged and the diagnostic and ventilation switches closed, the ratio of pilot voltage to battery voltage must lie between 0.05 and 0.10 in the 2011 table, or between 0.04 and 0.10 in the 2016 and 2019 tables. 30 failed samples out of 50 at 100 ms set it as Type A, MIL after one trip; the pilot circuit and charging switch tests must have finished first. Circuit faults are P0D00, P0D02 and P0D03. If the switch really sticks closed, stations without ventilation will not supply power.

causes.label: Internal fault in the VICM/charging module switching or measuring circuit
Ventilation resistor branch out of tolerance or high contact resistance
Leakage on the pilot line, for example moisture in the charge inlet

symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp on (GM Type A)
Charging possibly refused at stations without ventilation

P0D02.title: Control Pilot Charging Ventilation Switch Circuit Low
P0D02.description: P0D02 marks the control or feedback line of the ventilation switch as too low, usually a harness wire grounded somewhere along its route or a charging module driver that has failed shorted. That switch places a resistor of about 270 Ω across the pilot so that the level falls to roughly 3 V, the state in which a vehicle demands charging with ventilation. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM's Chevrolet Volt evaluates the same switch by the pilot level it causes (P0D01, ratio 0.04-0.10 in a self-test), and CARB requires plug-in vehicles to monitor the charging system. If the short holds the switch closed, a station without ventilation will refuse to deliver power; if it holds it open, the fault mostly shows only as a stored code. The high-side fault is P0D03, the open line P0D00.

causes.label: Ventilation switch control or feedback wire shorted to ground
Shorted driver stage in the charging control module
Corrosion in a connector bridging the line to ground

symptoms: Charging refused at stations without ventilation
Stored code without noticeable effect

P0D03.title: Control Pilot Charging Ventilation Switch Circuit High
P0D03.description: Here the line that drives or reports the ventilation switch reads above its valid range, which points to a short to a supply voltage or a driver stage that no longer switches. The ventilation switch is the vehicle-side element that requests charging with ventilation by loading the control pilot with roughly 270 Ω and lowering it to around 3 V. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; the closest documented test is P0D01 on the Chevrolet Volt, where GM judges the switch from the pilot voltage it produces in a self-test with the cord unplugged, and CARB requires plug-in vehicles to monitor the charging system. Low readings are P0D02, an open circuit P0D00, intermittent faults P0D04. Effects range from a stored code only to a refused charging session, depending on which switch state the fault forces.

causes.label: Ventilation switch control or feedback wire shorted to a supply voltage
Output stage in the charging module no longer switching
Lost ground at the switch letting the line float high

symptoms: Stored code, sometimes with a charging system warning
Charging refused if the switch is forced closed

P0D04.title: Control Pilot Charging Ventilation Switch Intermittent/Erratic
P0D04.description: P0D04 covers short, irregular disturbances in the ventilation switch circuit: the signal drops out or flickers, while lasting faults would be stored as P0D00, P0D02 or P0D03. Worn or corroded contacts in the charge inlet or module connector, and wires that lose contact under vibration, are the obvious suspects. Whenever the ventilation switch closes even briefly, it pulls the pilot toward about 3 V, so a station without ventilation suddenly sees a demand it cannot meet and may switch off. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM's Chevrolet Volt shows how the switch is checked via P0D01, and CARB requires plug-in vehicles to monitor the charging system. In practice the driver notices charging sessions that stop for no obvious reason and a code that comes back after clearing.

causes.label: Loose or spread terminal in the ventilation switch circuit
Corrosion or moisture in the charge inlet or module connector
Chafed wire with contact loss under vibration

symptoms: Charging sessions stop without obvious reason
Code returns after clearing

P0D05.title: Control Pilot Charging Ventilation Switch Stuck Off
P0D05.description: Stuck Off for the ventilation switch means the module commands the switch closed, yet the pilot does not drop to the level around 3 V that marks a request for charging with ventilation. Possible causes are a switch that no longer closes, an open resistor in the roughly 270 Ω branch, or a measuring fault in the module. Because ordinary charging takes place without a ventilation request, this fault rarely restricts charging; it mainly shows up during the self-test the module runs on the circuit. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM's Chevrolet Volt performs that kind of self-test as P0D01, with a normalized pilot voltage window of 0.04-0.10, and CARB requires plug-in vehicles to monitor the charging system. The opposite case is P0D06, circuit faults are P0D00 to P0D03. Expect a stored code and charging that still works.

causes.label: Ventilation switch in the module no longer closing
Open resistor or solder joint in the ventilation branch
Pilot measuring fault in the charging module

symptoms: Stored code, charging normally still possible
Charging system warning in the cluster on some vehicles

P0D06.title: Control Pilot Charging Ventilation Switch Stuck On
P0D06.description: Stuck On means the ventilation switch remains closed when it should be open, so the pilot is held near 3 V and the station reads a permanent demand for charging with ventilation. Stations that cannot provide ventilation do not supply power in that state, which in practice stops charging altogether. Likely causes are a welded or sticking switch, a short across the 270 Ω branch, or a module output that no longer releases. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM's Chevrolet Volt checks the same switch through P0D01 by the pilot level it causes in a self-test, and Mercedes-Benz documents the matching failure of charging switch A as P0CFE00 (switch not opening, cured by software). The counterpart is P0D05, circuit faults are P0D00 to P0D03. The car is detected at the station but does not charge.

causes.label: Ventilation switch contacts welded or sticking closed
Short across the ventilation resistor branch
Module output or software holding the switch on

symptoms: Charging station does not supply power
Charging error message after plugging in

P0D07.title: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor A Circuit
P0D07.description: P0D07 is the general circuit code for positive contactor A of the charging system, the switch that joins the plus side of a charging path to the traction battery. Depending on the design this path comes from the DC fast-charge inlet or from the on-board charger; the Chevrolet Volt, for instance, places charging contactors between charger and pack. The code stands for an electrical fault in that contactor branch which fits no more specific case. No manufacturer documents P0D07 publicly; a GM patent describes judging such contactors by their coil current, and CARB requires plug-in vehicles to monitor charging components. Welded or non-closing contacts are P0D08/P0D09, driver faults P0D0A–P0D0D, the main pack contactors P0AA0 ff. Usually charging is blocked while driving still works.

causes.label: Contactor coil open or shorted
Damaged wiring or corroded connector in the contactor branch
Fault in the module that drives and monitors the contactor

symptoms: Charging not possible or aborted
Charging system warning in the instrument cluster

P0D08.title: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor A Stuck Closed
P0D08.description: P0D08 means positive charging contactor A has stayed closed although the control module commanded it open, typically because the contacts have welded. The module notices this when voltage remains on the charging side, for instance at the charge port once a session has ended, as a Toyota patent on charge-relay sticking explains. GM stores P0D08 in the BECM of the 2023 Cadillac Lyriq; bulletin 23-NA-096 traces a joint setting with P0D0F to a software fault after an interrupted level 2 AC session and confirms it with a one-minute test charge. Stellantis lists P0D08-00 for the 2024–2025 Ram ProMaster EV with MIL and a vehicle that may not enable, remedied by BPCM reflash. The negative side is P0D0F, the opposite fault P0D09. A live inlet is a safety risk, so charging or driving gets locked out.

causes.label: Contactor contacts welded, for example after switching under load
Battery module software misjudging the contactor state (GM Lyriq, Ram ProMaster EV bulletins)
Driver stage or coil supply that does not switch off

symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp and high-voltage service message
Charging refused
Vehicle may not switch to ready mode

P0D09.title: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor A Stuck Open
P0D09.description: P0D09 is set when positive charging contactor A fails to close: after the command the expected voltage never shows up on the charger side. GM documents the check for the Chevrolet Volt (VICM 2016, HPC2 2019): during charger precharge, with charging and precharge contactors on and the negative main contactor still off, a charger voltage under 10 V ends the test; 2016 needs 8 failing samples out of 9, 2019 waits for at least 0.7 s of precharge. Both are Type A, MIL after one trip. Kia lists P0D0972 for the 2023 Niro EV (bulletin 298, ICCU replacement), Stellantis P0D09 for Wagoneer S and Charger Daytona (BPCM update), GM preliminary PIT6083 for the 2024 Lyriq after very long charging. Charging then stops or never starts; the welded case is P0D08.

causes.label: Contactor mechanically failing to close or burnt contacts
Fault in the on-board charger or integrated charging unit (Kia ICCU bulletin)
Control software needing an update (Stellantis, GM Lyriq)
Missing coil supply because of a wiring or fuse fault

symptoms: Charging does not start or ends shortly after plugging in
Malfunction indicator lamp after one trip (GM Type A)
Charging or high-voltage warning in the cluster

P0D0A.title: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor A Control Circuit/Open
P0D0A.description: P0D0A covers the drive circuit of positive charging contactor A: the module compares the commanded state of its driver with the voltage and current it actually sees on the coil line. GM spells this out for the Chevrolet Volt and Cadillac ELR: with the driver off, an output above 4 V means an open line and one close to supply voltage a short to power; with the driver on, coil current below 57 mA (Volt 2019: 194 mA) also counts as open. 40 of 50 samples at 12.5 ms set the code. The 2011 and 2014 Volt and the ELR rate it Type A, the 2016 and 2019 Volt Type B with MIL after two trips. GM adds that the test cannot see a short to ground. Range/performance, low and high are P0D0B–P0D0D. Without a working contactor the car will not charge.

causes.label: Open or high-resistance coil control wire or connector
Contactor coil open
Control wire shorted to a supply voltage
Faulty high-side driver in the control module

symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp (GM Type A or B)
Vehicle does not charge

P0D0B.title: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor A Control Circuit Range/Performance
P0D0B.description: P0D0B reports that the control circuit of positive charging contactor A works electrically but does not behave plausibly – coil current or line voltage outside the window expected for the commanded state, or a response that comes too slowly. No manufacturer documents P0D0B publicly. The nearest documented test is GM's P0D0A on the Chevrolet Volt, which matches commanded and actual driver state and judges coil current, and CARB requires plug-in vehicles to check charging components for circuit and rationality faults. Typical triggers are contact resistance in connectors, a coil whose resistance has drifted, or a weakening driver stage. Opens are P0D0A, low and high signals P0D0C/P0D0D, mechanical sticking P0D08/P0D09. Charging may work only now and then or be refused.

causes.label: Contact resistance or corrosion in the control circuit connectors
Contactor coil with changed resistance
Weakening driver stage in the control module

symptoms: Charging sessions fail sporadically
Stored code, possibly with a charging system warning

P0D0C.title: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor A Control Circuit Low
P0D0C.description: P0D0C stands for a control line of positive charging contactor A that reads too low, usually a short to ground or a driver output pulled down. When the coil is fed through a high-side driver, a grounded line leaves the contactor without power or overloads the driver. No manufacturer documents P0D0C publicly. GM states that its own Volt check for this contactor, P0D0A, cannot detect a short to ground, so the documented tests do not cover this case; CARB requires the charging system of plug-in vehicles to be monitored. Chafed harness sections near the battery or charge inlet and water in connectors are the usual causes. High readings are P0D0D, opens P0D0A, the negative side P0D13. The typical result is a charging session that will not start.

causes.label: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Moisture in a connector creating a path to ground
Shorted contactor coil

symptoms: Charging does not start
Charging system warning

P0D0D.title: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor A Control Circuit High
P0D0D.description: P0D0D means the control line of positive charging contactor A sits too high, typically from a short to a supply voltage or a driver that no longer switches off. The coil may then stay energised, so the contactor could close without a command, which the module has to prevent. No manufacturer documents P0D0D publicly; on the Chevrolet Volt GM folds the short to power into P0D0A and flags it when the off-state output stays within 0.4 V of supply. CARB requires plug-in vehicles to monitor charging components. Causes are crossed or chafed wiring and a failed driver inside the control module. Low readings are P0D0C, opens P0D0A, a welded contactor P0D08. The system normally blocks charging until the fault is gone.

causes.label: Control wire shorted to a supply voltage
Driver stage in the control module stuck on
Open ground return of the coil letting the line float high

symptoms: Charging blocked
Charging or high-voltage system warning

P0D0E.title: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor A Circuit
P0D0E.description: P0D0E is the general circuit code for negative contactor A of the charging system, which connects the minus side of the charging path – from DC inlet or on-board charger – to the traction battery. It is used when the module sees an electrical fault on that contactor that it does not classify more precisely. No manufacturer documents P0D0E publicly. A GM patent on battery disconnect diagnosis shows separate contactor pairs for fast and slow charging and judges each by its coil current, and CARB requires plug-in vehicles to monitor charging components. Welding or failure to close on the negative side are P0D0F/P0D10, driver faults P0D11–P0D14, the positive side P0D07, the main pack contactors P0AA3 ff. In most cases only charging is affected.

causes.label: Contactor coil open or shorted
Damaged wiring or corroded connector in the contactor branch
Fault in the module that drives and monitors the contactor

symptoms: Charging not possible or aborted
Charging system warning in the instrument cluster

P0D0F.title: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor A Stuck Closed
P0D0F.description: P0D0F flags negative charging contactor A as stuck closed: it still conducts after the open command, usually through welded contacts or a misjudged state. Ford stores it in the BECM of the 2021–2022 Mustang Mach-E together with main-contactor codes such as P0AA1 and P0AA4; bulletins 22-2178 and 23-2020 replace the high-voltage battery junction box and reprogram the BECM, and a flat 12 V battery or the Stop Safely Now warning may accompany it. Stellantis lists P0D0F-00 for the Grand Cherokee 4xe with a MIL, partly a false alarm, and cures it with BPCM software (0817922, 08-006-25). GM sets it together with P0D08 on the 2023 Lyriq after an interrupted AC session (23-NA-096). A Toyota patent checks such sticking via charge-port voltage. The positive side is P0D08, the opposite fault P0D10.

causes.label: Faulty high-voltage battery junction box with the charging contactors (Ford Mach-E)
Battery module software misjudging the contactor (Stellantis 4xe, GM Lyriq)
Welded contactor contacts

symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp or wrench lamp
Stop Safely Now message or no ready mode (Ford)
Discharged 12 V battery

P0D10.title: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor A Stuck Open
P0D10.description: P0D10 means negative charging contactor A does not close when told to, so the charging path never gets its return line and the session fails. Ford names it in the BECM of the 2021–2023 Mustang Mach-E next to main-contactor codes; the bulletins (23-2020, 23-2257) replace the high-voltage battery junction box and update the BECM. GM's preliminary PIT6083 for the 2024 Lyriq links P0D09 and P0D10 to very long charging sessions and advises disconnecting the cord once a day for 20 minutes or more until new software arrives. Stellantis lists both codes for the Wagoneer S and Charger Daytona, where a no-start can follow, and handles them with BPCM updates. Welding on this side is P0D0F, the control circuit P0D11, the positive counterpart P0D09. Expect charging to stop.

causes.label: Faulty high-voltage battery junction box with the charging contactors (Ford Mach-E)
Battery module software needing an update (GM Lyriq, Stellantis)
Contactor failing to close or burnt contacts

symptoms: Charging does not start or stops
Malfunction indicator lamp and high-voltage service message
Vehicle may not start (Lyriq, Stellantis)

P0D11.title: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor A Control Circuit/Open
P0D11.description: P0D11 is the open-circuit and driver check for negative charging contactor A. GM uses it on the Chevrolet Volt (2011, 2014) and the Cadillac ELR: the module compares the commanded driver state with what the line shows; with the driver off, an output above 4 V (2011: 2 V) means open and one close to supply voltage a short to power, and with the driver on a coil current below 57 mA is judged open as well. 40 failing samples out of 50 at 12.5 ms set it as Type A, MIL after one trip; the status of the charging HVIL source is part of the enable conditions. As on the positive side, a short to ground lies outside this test. The positive counterpart is P0D0A, plausibility, low and high are P0D12–P0D14. The vehicle will not charge.

causes.label: Open or high-resistance coil control wire or connector
Contactor coil open
Control wire shorted to a supply voltage
Faulty driver stage in the control module

symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp after one trip (GM Type A)
Vehicle does not charge

P0D12.title: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor A Control Circuit Range/Performance
P0D12.description: P0D12 points to a control circuit of negative charging contactor A that is electrically intact yet implausible: current, voltage or switching response do not fit the command. No manufacturer documents P0D12 publicly. GM's closest test is P0D11 on the Chevrolet Volt and Cadillac ELR, comparing driver command with line state and coil current, and CARB requires plug-in vehicles to monitor charging components for rationality faults in addition to circuit faults. Corroded terminals, a coil whose resistance has shifted and poor grounds are the usual suspects. Opens fall under P0D11, low and high signals under P0D13/P0D14, the positive side under P0D0B. Charging may drop out or refuse to begin.

causes.label: Contact resistance or corrosion in the control circuit connectors
Contactor coil with shifted resistance
Poor ground of the control module or coil return

symptoms: Charging sessions fail sporadically
Stored code, possibly with a charging system warning

P0D13.title: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor A Control Circuit Low
P0D13.description: P0D13 means the control line of negative charging contactor A reads too low, which points to a short to ground or a driver output held down. The coil then receives no current, or too little, and the contactor stays open. No manufacturer documents P0D13 publicly; GM notes that its P0D11 test for this contactor on the Volt and ELR cannot detect a short to ground, and CARB requires plug-in vehicles to monitor charging components. Typical causes are a wire chafed against the body or battery housing and moisture inside a connector. P0D14 is the high counterpart, P0D11 the open circuit, P0D0C the same fault on the positive side. In practice the vehicle refuses to charge.

causes.label: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Moisture in a connector creating a path to ground
Shorted contactor coil

symptoms: Vehicle refuses to charge
Charging system warning

P0D14.title: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor A Control Circuit High
P0D14.description: P0D14 is set when the control line of negative charging contactor A reads too high, for example through a short to the 12 V supply or a driver stage that will not switch off. That can keep the coil energised and the contactor closed without a command, so the module blocks charging. No manufacturer documents P0D14 publicly; on the Volt and ELR GM counts a short to power under P0D11 and detects it when the off-state output stays close to supply voltage. CARB requires plug-in vehicles to monitor charging components. Chafed or crossed wiring and a failed driver are the main causes. The low case is P0D13, a welded contactor P0D0F, the positive side P0D0D. Repairs belong in the hands of high-voltage trained staff.

causes.label: Control wire shorted to a supply voltage
Driver stage in the control module stuck on
Open ground return of the coil letting the line float high

symptoms: Charging blocked
Charging or high-voltage system warning

P0D15.title: Battery Charging System A High Voltage Interlock Circuit/Open
P0D15.description: P0D15 reports an open high-voltage interlock loop in charging system A. This low-voltage loop runs through the connectors and covers of the charging path – inlet, charger and their HV leads – and breaks as soon as one of them is unplugged, so the module can keep that path de-energised. It is separate from the interlock of battery and drive, which uses P0A0A ff. Volvo stores P0D1513 in the on-board charger of the 2021–2023 XC40 Recharge when AC charging fails; bulletin TJ 36522 blames catches on the AC HV connector between inlet and charger that were not fully closed at the plant and has the connector reseated and latched. GM's Volt and ELR monitor such a charging loop with a 5 V source, and a Ford patent describes interlock shorting bars in connectors. Other loop faults are P0D16–P0D19.

causes.label: HV connector in the charging path not fully seated or latched (Volvo XC40)
Broken interlock wire or pushed-back terminal
Missing or loose cover on a charging component

symptoms: AC charging not possible
Charge inlet light indicates a fault

P0D16.title: Battery Charging System A High Voltage Interlock Circuit Performance
P0D16.description: P0D16 flags a charging interlock loop that delivers a signal, just not the one expected – for example a reading that fails to follow when the module switches its test source on and off. No manufacturer documents P0D16 publicly. GM's Chevrolet Volt and Cadillac ELR show how such a loop is checked: the module feeds 5 V into the charging HVIL and compares the sensed level, as a share of the reference, against limits with the source on and off, which leads to P0D17 or P0D18. A Ford patent explains interlock loops built from shorting bars in connectors. Contact resistance in a connector, a plug inserted only partway and corrosion are typical. Open loops are P0D15, sporadic faults P0D19, the drive-side counterpart P0A0B. Charging is usually blocked.

causes.label: Contact resistance or corrosion in an interlock connector
HV connector in the charging path inserted only partway
Fault in the module's interlock source or measuring stage

symptoms: Charging refused
Charging system warning

P0D17.title: Battery Charging System A High Voltage Interlock Circuit Low
P0D17.description: P0D17 means the sensed voltage of the charging HVIL loop is too low. GM documents the check for the Chevrolet Volt (2011, 2014) and the Cadillac ELR: while the module sources 5 V into the loop, a sensed value under 30 % of the reference in two samples out of two at 12.5 ms sets the code as Type A, with the MIL on after one trip. A low reading suggests a path to ground or leakage somewhere in the loop wiring, or a fault in the measuring stage of the module. Because the test only runs with the source switched on, it typically shows up around charging. The interlock of battery and drive has its own code, P0A0C. P0D18 is the high counterpart, P0D15 the open loop. With an implausible loop the car refuses to charge.

causes.label: Interlock wire chafed and touching ground
Moisture or dirt in an interlock connector causing leakage
Fault in the interlock source or measuring circuit of the control module

symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp after one trip (GM Type A)
Charging refused

P0D18.title: Battery Charging System A High Voltage Interlock Circuit High
P0D18.description: P0D18 flags a charging HVIL signal that sits too high. On the Chevrolet Volt and Cadillac ELR GM tests the loop in two states: with the 5 V source off, a sensed level above 24 % of reference (5 of 6 samples in 2011, 5 of 8 for 2014 and ELR), and with it on, a level above 44 % (4 of 6), set the code as Type A, MIL after one trip. A high value may point to a break or added resistance in the loop or a short to a voltage. Polestar stores P0D1800 in the BECM of the 2021–2023 Polestar 2 with a propulsion warning and resolves it with BECM software 2.10 (TJ 36713). Kia lists P0D1812 for the 2023 Niro EV among the codes that lead to ICCU replacement (bulletin 298). The low case is P0D17, the open loop P0D15.

causes.label: High resistance or partial break in the interlock loop
Battery module software needing an update (Polestar 2)
Faulty integrated charging unit (Kia Niro EV ICCU)
Interlock wire shorted to a voltage source

symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp (GM Type A)
Propulsion or high-voltage warning in the cluster
Slow or no AC charging

P0D19.title: Battery Charging System A High Voltage Interlock Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0D19.description: P0D19 covers a charging interlock loop that drops out and comes back, so the signal flips between valid and invalid within a short time. Loose terminals, a connector that is not fully latched, a chafing wire that only touches over bumps and vibration-sensitive solder joints are typical causes. No manufacturer documents P0D19 publicly. GM's Volt and ELR tables show the checks applied to the same loop, namely low and high limits on the sensed share of a 5 V reference, and a Ford patent explains why intermittent interlock contacts matter and how a loop can be arranged so a brief interruption does not cut propulsion. CARB requires plug-in vehicles to monitor charging components. Steady faults are P0D15–P0D18, the drive interlock intermittent code is P0A0E. Charging may stop without warning.

causes.label: Loose or spread terminal in an interlock connector
HV connector in the charging path not fully latched
Chafed interlock wire making contact only under vibration

symptoms: Charging stops unexpectedly
Intermittent charging system warning

P0D1A.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve B Control Circuit/Open
P0D1A.description: P0D1A flags an open or otherwise faulty drive circuit of coolant control valve B, a second actuator in the coolant loop of the hybrid or EV battery. Which physical valve gets the letter B, and what it switches, is up to the vehicle maker. No manufacturer documents P0D1A in a public bulletin or OBD table. The best documented analogue is valve A: Mercedes battery management reports its actuation as faulty or interrupted (LI83.30-P-061224), and CARB requires every electronic output used for battery heating or cooling to be checked for circuit faults. A broken wire, a corroded plug or an open valve coil are the usual findings. With the valve unusable the pack may run too warm or too cold, so charging and power can be limited. Shorts to ground or voltage are P0D1D and P0D1E.

causes.label: Broken wire or corroded connector in the valve B drive circuit
Open coil or motor winding inside valve B
Faulty output stage in the controlling module

symptoms: Hybrid or EV system warning and MIL
Reduced charging or drive power because battery temperature cannot be managed

P0D1B.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve B Performance/Stuck Off
P0D1B.description: P0D1B is stored when coolant control valve B of the battery loop is electrically intact but fails to reach or hold the position the controller asks for, or stays in its off state. How a maker judges this varies: for valve A, GM's 2011 Chevrolet Volt learns the end stops, expects the target within 1.5 s and watches for drift above 3 %, while Audi and Toyota infer a wrong valve state from coolant temperatures. No such table or bulletin is published for valve B, so P0D1B appears in no public manufacturer document. CARB asks for a functional check of battery cooling performance wherever feasible. Debris, a seized valve body, a worn actuator or a calibration that judges too tightly are plausible. Cooling or heating of the pack then suffers. The opposite case is P0D1C.

causes.label: Valve B mechanically stiff or blocked by debris
Worn valve actuator that no longer reaches its target
Diagnostic limits in the module software set too tightly
Low coolant or trapped air distorting the temperature-based check

symptoms: MIL or battery thermal system warning
Battery temperature rises during fast charging or hard driving
Charging or drive power limited

P0D1C.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve B Stuck On
P0D1C.description: P0D1C means coolant control valve B of the battery circuit remains in its active position although the controller has commanded a change. What active means depends on the design: on valve A, Mercedes hybrid battery management distinguishes a shutoff valve that will not close (P0CE000) from one that will not open (P0CE100), which shows that makers map on and off to opposite valve states. For valve B no manufacturer publishes P0D1C in a bulletin or OBD table. Where feasible, CARB wants the parts that heat or cool the battery checked for proper function. A jammed valve, a driver that never switches off, or software misjudging the temperature response are plausible causes. Coolant then keeps flowing through the wrong path, so the pack may be overcooled or heated poorly. The opposite fault is P0D1B.

causes.label: Valve B jammed in its active position
Output stage or supply that keeps the valve energised
Module software misjudging the temperature response of the loop

symptoms: MIL or battery thermal system warning
Battery warms slowly in cold weather or charging is slower than usual

P0D1D.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve B Control Circuit Low
P0D1D.description: P0D1D reports that the drive line of coolant control valve B reads too low, which normally means a short to ground. No manufacturer publishes P0D1D itself. The closest documented test is GM's check of valve A in the 2011 Chevrolet Volt and the 2016 Cadillac ELR: the motor-driven valve has two driver lines, and a low reading on line 1 while the valve should run in reverse, with system voltage above 9 V or 10.2 V, sets the code after 90 failed samples out of 100; it is Type B, which lights the MIL only on the second trip. A comparable logic is to be expected for B. Typical findings are a wire chafed through to the body, water in a connector or an internal short in the valve motor. While active, the valve stays where it is. Short to voltage is P0D1E, open circuit P0D1A.

causes.label: Valve B driver wire chafed and shorted to ground
Moisture or corrosion in the valve connector
Internal short in the valve motor

symptoms: MIL after two trips (where the maker uses a two-trip code)
Battery cooling or heating restricted, charging or power limited

P0D1E.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve B Control Circuit High
P0D1E.description: P0D1E is the short-to-voltage counterpart for coolant control valve B: the controller sees its drive line high at a moment when it should be low. P0D1E is not described in any public manufacturer document. For valve A, GM documents the matching test on the Chevrolet Volt 2011 and Cadillac ELR 2016: driver line 1 reads high while the valve should be stopped or moving forward, system voltage above 9 V or 10.2 V, 90 out of 100 checks, Type B with the lamp lit on the second trip. Because the check runs in the opposite direction of travel to the low test, the stored code already hints at which wire is affected. Pinched wires touching a supply line or a driver stage that will not switch off are the usual suspects. Battery temperature control falls back to a default. Short to ground is P0D1D, open circuit P0D1A.

causes.label: Valve B driver wire pinched against a supply line
Output stage in the controlling module stuck high
Damaged or contaminated connector bridging two pins

symptoms: MIL after two trips (where the maker uses a two-trip code)
Battery thermal management in fallback mode, charging or power limited

P0D1F.title: Control Module Date/Time Synchronization Error
P0D1F.description: P0D1F says a control module could not align its internal date and time with the reference the rest of the vehicle uses. Hybrid modules need a trustworthy clock because several checks depend on how long the car has been parked: CARB, for example, ties cold-start monitoring to at least six hours off, and GM separately checks its module power-off timer against the on-timer (P262B, more than 5.6 % deviation on the 2012 Volt). Volvo stores P0D1F62 in the BECM of its long-range plug-in hybrids from 2022 to 2024 with the check engine light on. Journals TJ 36681 and TJ 36707 call it a misdetection, rule out parts replacement and prescribe BECM software 2.11. If P0D1F96 follows the update, the car must sleep at least 15 minutes to resync its timers before the code is erased.

causes.label: Module software misdetecting the time comparison (Volvo BECM software 2.11)
Timers not yet resynchronised after programming because the car has not slept
Missing or wrong time information from the module providing the reference clock

symptoms: Check engine light without a noticeable driving fault
Code returns as a variant after a software update until the car has slept

P0D20.title: Battery Charger A Output Voltage Performance
P0D20.description: P0D20 concerns the on-board charger in its constant-voltage phase, typically near the end of a charge, when it should hold its high-voltage output at a set value. The code means the measured output voltage strays too far from that target. GM's 2011 to 2013 Chevrolet Volt evaluates this in the HPC2/VICM: a deviation of 15 % or more in constant-voltage mode, counted at 100 ms with system voltage above 9 V (2011) or 10.2 V (2012), sets the code after 30 failures in 50 samples, One Trip Type A, so the MIL comes on at once. Later GM tables no longer list it. CARB requires charger faults that stop or slow charging to be detected. Causes lie mostly inside the charger or its voltage sensing. Charging stops or ends early; driving is unaffected. Too low a voltage is P0D21.

causes.label: Fault in the charger's power stage or voltage control
Inaccurate output voltage measurement
Charge control software in the hybrid control module

symptoms: Charging stops early or the battery does not reach its target level
MIL and charging system message

P0D21.title: Battery Charger A Output Voltage Too Low
P0D21.description: P0D21 is set when the high-voltage output of the on-board charger stays below what the controller expects. GM's Volt and ELR tables split the test in two: during normal charging the charger bus must not fall under 150 V, and when the charger only powers the battery heater, the bus must reach at least 75 % of an expected value calculated from charger current times 70 ohms. Eight failures in ten samples store it as Type B, lighting the MIL on the second trip. Stellantis stores P0D21-00 in the integrated dual charging module (IDCM) of the Jeep Wrangler 4xe from 2021, the Grand Cherokee 4xe from 2022 and the Pacifica Plug-in Hybrid from 2022, with MIL and no charging, and reflashes the IDCM. P0D20 covers a deviation in constant-voltage mode, P0D85 excess voltage.

causes.label: Charger module software (Stellantis IDCM bulletins)
Failing power stage inside the charger
High resistance or fault in the charger's high-voltage output path or heater load

symptoms: Vehicle does not charge
MIL, often after two charging trips
Battery not preheated while plugged in during cold weather

P0D22.title: Battery Charger A Output Current Performance
P0D22.description: P0D22 means the on-board charger does not deliver the high-voltage current it was asked for. GM's Volt compares actual and desired current in constant-current mode against a table: 150 of 300 samples set it in 2011, One Trip Type A; from 2014 a second part also catches a charger that was switched on, with more than 201 V commanded, but never enabled its output after 6 s. Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV stops charging when target and actual differ by 3 A or more for 3 s. GM bulletins cite P0D22 with MIL and no charge on the 2011 and 2013 Volt (HPCM2 updates) and, in PIP6048, on the Lyriq, Optiq, Blazer EV and Equinox EV during level 2 charging, where reprogramming the BECM comes first. Voltage deviations belong to P0D20/P0D21, a shorted output to P0D23.

causes.label: Charge control software in the hybrid or battery control module (GM PIP bulletins)
Internal fault in the on-board charger
Faulty output current measurement

symptoms: Vehicle does not charge or charging stops
MIL on after a charge session ends
Problem shows mainly on AC level 2 stations

P0D23.title: Battery Charger A Output Shorted
P0D23.description: P0D23 points to a short on the high-voltage output side of the on-board charger. GM runs this check while the charger contactor is only in its precharge state and the multi-purpose contactor is open, a moment when almost no current should flow on the charger bus. If more than 0.35 A is measured there in four of five samples at 100 ms, with system voltage above 9 V or 10.2 V, the code is set as One Trip Type A in the Chevrolet Volt from 2011 and the Cadillac ELR up to 2016. The test is skipped while output current sensor faults are active or while thermal conditioning runs. A current at that stage suggests an internal short in the charger output, a damaged high-voltage cable or a stuck contactor path. Charging is blocked. Current deviations during normal charging are P0D22.

causes.label: Internal short in the charger's high-voltage output stage
Damaged high-voltage cable between charger and battery
Charging contactor path conducting when it should not

symptoms: Charging refused immediately after plugging in
MIL on at once

P0D24.title: Battery Charger A Temperature Too High
P0D24.description: P0D24 is stored when the on-board charger reports an internal temperature above its permitted limit. Chargers protect themselves by reducing power or stopping, so the driver typically notices slow or interrupted AC charging. Kia lists P0D2498, failure type 98 for over-temperature, among the codes of the integrated charging control unit (ICCU) in bulletin 298 for the 2023 Niro EV: poor or no charging on level 1 or level 2 while DC fast charging still works, sometimes with MIL and warning messages; after checking the 12 V battery and other conditions, the ICCU is replaced. CARB requires plug-in hybrids to detect charger faults that prevent or slow charging. Besides an internal defect, a weak cooling path, low coolant or a blocked air flow can drive the temperature up. Cooling system performance is P0D8F.

causes.label: Internal defect in the charger or charging control unit (Kia ICCU replacement)
Low coolant, failed pump or blocked air flow on the charger cooling path
Charger temperature sensor reading too high

symptoms: AC charging slow, interrupted or impossible while DC fast charging works
Warning message for the electric system, sometimes MIL

P0D25.title: Battery Charger System Precharge Time Too Short
P0D25.description: P0D25 is about the precharge of the charger's high-voltage bus, the short phase before the charging contactors close in which the bus capacitance is brought up to battery voltage through a limiting path. The code means this voltage arrived sooner than physically plausible. No manufacturer documents P0D25 publicly. GM describes the counterpart test for the charger bus under P0D26, with a window of 5 % around pack voltage, and the same principle for the main battery under P0C77, where the 2011 Volt flags a rise above 95 % within 50 ms. A rise that quick suggests a bypassed precharge resistor, a contactor that is welded or closes early, missing bus capacitance or a voltage sensor reporting wrong values. CARB requires charger faults that affect charging to be detected. Charging is normally refused.

causes.label: Precharge resistor bypassed or shorted
Charging contactor welded or closing too early
Bus or pack voltage sensor reporting wrong values
Bus capacitance much lower than expected

symptoms: Charging refused at the start of a session
Charging system warning

P0D26.title: Battery Charger System Precharge Time Too Long
P0D26.description: P0D26 means the charger's high-voltage bus did not come up to battery voltage within the allowed precharge time. GM's Volt 2011 to 2015 and ELR 2014 to 2016 require the bus to sit within 5 % of pack voltage for 0.25 s before 10 s have passed; the 2016 and 2017 Volt allow only 0.700 s to reach 95 % (later 95 to 105 %); all are One Trip Type A. Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV looks at the charger's own capacitor, which must charge to 120 or 240 V within 45 s, otherwise charging stops. Bulletin PIP4905E links P0D26 on the Volt and ELR to no charging and asks for HPCM2 software, then a check of the proximity signal and charge port for water or corrosion; on the Bolt EV (18-NA-225) it comes with P0C78 when the fuse in the manual disconnect has opened. The main battery precharge is P0C78.

causes.label: Open precharge resistor, fuse or contactor in the precharge path
Blown fuse in the manual service disconnect (Bolt EV bulletin)
Erratic proximity signal from a wet or corroded charge port
Outdated hybrid control module software

symptoms: Vehicle does not charge on 120 V or 240 V
MIL on at once
With a blown disconnect fuse, loss of propulsion

P0D27.title: Battery Charger Input Voltage Too Low
P0D27.description: P0D27 says the AC voltage reaching the on-board charger sits lower than the charger accepts while charging is permitted. Unlike most charger codes, the cause often lies outside the car. Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV stops charging and tells technicians to check, in order, the customer's power supply, the charging cable, the high-voltage wiring between charge inlet and charger and finally the charger itself. Stellantis lists P0D27-00 as Battery Charger 1 Input Voltage Too Low in the integrated dual charging module of the 2021 Jeep Wrangler 4xe, with MIL, no level 2 charging and in some cases a tripping house breaker; the remedy is new IDCM software along with several other modules. Later notes ask for a test charge after clearing before an IDCM is replaced. Too high an input voltage is P0D28.

causes.label: Weak or overloaded AC supply at the charging location
Faulty charging cable or EVSE
Charger module software (Stellantis IDCM reflash)
Damaged wiring or loose contact between charge inlet and charger

symptoms: AC charging does not start or stops
House circuit breaker trips when plugging in
MIL

P0D28.title: Battery Charger Input Voltage Too High
P0D28.description: P0D28 is the mirror case of P0D27: the AC voltage at the charger input lies above the range the charger can accept. Mitsubishi evaluates both on the Outlander PHEV while the PHEV-ECU allows charging; the charger then stops and the technician works from the outside in, beginning with the supply and the charging cable, then the wiring between inlet and charger, and only last the charger. A real overvoltage is rare on public grids, so a faulty voltage measurement or software is often more likely. Audi lists P0D2800, battery charger primary voltage too high, among ghost DTCs stored by software 0088 in the high-voltage charger module of the e-tron and Q8 e-tron (2021-2024); bulletin 2062631 says to leave them unrepaired unless a charging complaint exists. Sensor faults are P0D3E-P0D40.

causes.label: Input voltage sensing inside the charger reading too high
Charger software storing the code without a real fault (Audi ghost DTC)
Actual overvoltage or unstable supply at the charging location
Faulty charging cable or EVSE

symptoms: AC charging stops or does not start
Code found in memory without any complaint

P0D29.title: Battery Charger Input Current Too Low
P0D29.description: P0D29 is set when the on-board charger draws less AC current than expected for the power it was asked to deliver, while voltage and charging permission are present. No manufacturer documents P0D29 publicly. Related tests show how such a check is built: GM's Volt compares the AC input current with fixed limits for the high side (P0D2A), and Mitsubishi first verifies that the input current sensor reads plausibly before trusting it (P0D39). A low current with normal voltage points to a charger that does not ramp up, high resistance at the inlet or cable, an EVSE that limits current, or a measurement fault. CARB requires charger faults that limit the charging rate to be detected. Charging is slower than usual or stops. Too much current is P0D2A, voltage problems P0D27/P0D28.

causes.label: Charger power stage not ramping up
High resistance at the charge inlet, cable or plug contacts
Input current sensor reading too low
Charging station or cable limiting current more than signalled

symptoms: AC charging much slower than usual
Charging stops or charging system warning

P0D2A.title: Battery Charger Input Current Too High
P0D2A.description: P0D2A reports that the on-board charger draws more AC input current than allowed. GM's Volt and ELR use two limits: more than 17 A at 185 V or above, more than 13 A below 185 V; 240 failures in 300 samples set it as One Trip Type A. The code is used widely: Stellantis (Battery Charger 1, Jeep Renegade and Compass PHEV 2020-2021, IDCM reflash with pilot codes P0CF3/P0CF4), Ford (2021 Mustang Mach-E, MIL from PCM parameters, TSB 22-2034, module reprogramming), Toyota and Lexus (P0D2A19 with PFC boost fault P1C1B00 on the RAV4 Prime with 6.6 kW charger and the NX 450h+, charger replacement), Kia (2023 Niro EV ICCU) and the newer Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV. Charging stops, often with MIL. Too little current is P0D29.

causes.label: Fault in the charger's input or PFC stage (Toyota/Lexus charger replacement)
Charger or powertrain module software (Stellantis, Ford bulletins)
Input current sensor reading too high

symptoms: AC charging stops shortly after starting
MIL on
On-board charging inoperative while DC charging may still work

P0D2B.title: Control Pilot Indicator Control Circuit/Open
P0D2B.description: P0D2B concerns the driver circuit of the control pilot indicator, a lamp or LED with which the vehicle signals the state of the pilot connection to the charging station. The code covers the lamp's own wiring, not the pilot signal itself. GM monitors it on the Chevrolet Volt and Cadillac ELR in two cases: a short to ground is detected while the LED is commanded on (12 bad readings out of 15), a short to battery or an open circuit while it is off and the cord is plugged in (40 out of 50), each sampled every 100 ms. The 2011 and 2012 Volt treat it as Type B with MIL after two trips; the 2016 ELR tables list One Trip Type A. Wiring damage, a failed LED or a bad connector are the likely causes. Charging itself usually continues. Faults of the pilot line are P0CF3 and P0CF4.

causes.label: Damaged wiring or loose connector to the indicator
Failed indicator LED
Faulty LED driver in the controlling module

symptoms: Indicator stays dark or lit regardless of charging state
MIL, depending on model after one or two trips

P0D2C.title: Charge Status Indicator A Control Circuit/Open
P0D2C.description: P0D2C is set for a fault in the driver circuit of charge status indicator A, the light that tells the driver whether the car is charging. On the Chevrolet Volt that light is part of the diagnosis itself: bulletin PIP4905E has technicians watch whether the charge indicator on the instrument panel stays steady green. GM tests the driver for a ground short while the LED is commanded on and for a short to battery or an open circuit while it is off, needing 40 bad readings out of 50 at 100 ms. Volt 2011 and 2012 set the code as Type B, with the MIL on the second trip; the 2016 ELR tables use One Trip Type A. A broken wire, a failed LED or a corroded plug are typical. Charging still works, but the owner loses the visual confirmation. A second indicator B uses P0DE5.

causes.label: Broken wire or corroded connector to the indicator
Failed charge status LED
Faulty LED driver in the controlling module

symptoms: Charge status light dark or permanently lit
MIL, depending on model after one or two trips

P0D2D.title: Drive Motor A Inverter Voltage Sensor A Circuit
P0D2D.description: Drive motor A's inverter measures the DC link voltage it switches, and voltage sensor A is the channel that passes this value to the motor controller. P0D2D is the general circuit fault for that channel: the signal is missing or electrically unusable, without a more specific low or high verdict. Ford lists P0D2D among its MIL codes. On 2021 Mustang Mach-E vehicles it could be stored in secondary on-board control module C after charging, when a remote start ended in a no-start; customer satisfaction program 21B02 cured this with new software for the PCM and associated modules. Without a trusted bus voltage the controller usually limits or blocks electric drive. Plausibility faults are P0D2E, low and high signals P0D2F/P0D30, short dropouts P0D31.

causes.label: Inverter or powertrain module software fault (Ford 21B02)
Loose connector or damaged signal wiring of the voltage sensor
Voltage sensing circuit inside the inverter failed

symptoms: Hybrid or EV system warning and MIL
Vehicle does not become ready to drive or electric drive is reduced
No start after charging and remote start (Mach-E)

P0D2E.title: Drive Motor A Inverter Voltage Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0D2E.description: P0D2E means the inverter voltage reading of drive motor A is electrically valid but disagrees with other measurements of the same high-voltage bus. Mitsubishi shows the logic for the 2023 Outlander PHEV: with voltage control active, the power drive unit compares capacitor 1 with the rear motor unit and with both channels of capacitor 2; a gap of 100 V or 50 V held for 0.2 s sets the code, and an implausible PWM period counts too; the MIL comes on. Mercedes lists P0D2E00 in the battery management of its 2024 P3 plug-in hybrids (series 206, 223, 254, 290) when the high-voltage belt starter-alternator has failed and the engine no longer starts. So a drifting sensor and a real fault elsewhere on the bus are both possible. Hard circuit faults are P0D2D, P0D2F and P0D30.

causes.label: Voltage sensing in the power drive unit drifts or reads wrong
Fault in another HV component, e.g. belt starter-alternator (Mercedes)
High resistance or loose high-voltage connection between modules

symptoms: MIL and hybrid system warning
Engine will not start, only electric driving possible (Mercedes)
Reduced drive power

P0D2F.title: Drive Motor A Inverter Voltage Sensor A Circuit Low
P0D2F.description: P0D2F reports that the signal of inverter voltage sensor A for drive motor A sits at the bottom of its range, typical of an open circuit, a short to ground or no high voltage at all. In the 2018 Outlander PHEV Mitsubishi sets it in the front motor control unit when the sensor output stays below 0.5 V, equal to about 10 V on the bus, for 0.3 s while the propulsion system is active. The manual then checks the high-voltage fuse and the HV cabling before replacing the power drive unit, so a blown fuse or an open supply path can look like a sensor fault. The 2023 model uses 0.3 V at capacitor 1 for 0.16 s and lights the MIL. Expect the hybrid warning and loss of electric drive. The high side is P0D30.

causes.label: Blown high-voltage fuse or disconnected HV cable
Voltage sensing in the power drive unit failed (open or short to ground)
High-voltage battery delivers no voltage

symptoms: MIL and hybrid system warning
Vehicle not ready to drive or electric drive unavailable

P0D30.title: Drive Motor A Inverter Voltage Sensor A Circuit High
P0D30.description: P0D30 is the high-side partner of P0D2F: the inverter voltage signal of drive motor A stays near its upper limit. Mitsubishi checks it on the 2018 Outlander PHEV with the front motor unit supplied at 8 to 16 V; a sensor output above 4.7 V, which stands for roughly 440 V, for 0.3 s sets the code. The manual first asks whether the rear motor unit also stores P0DA6, because then a genuine overvoltage from the battery or the HV circuit is more likely than one bad sensor; fuse and cabling come next, the power drive unit last. The 2023 model uses 4.05 V at capacitor 1 for 0.16 s and turns on the MIL. A short to the sensor supply is the classic cause on the sensing side. Real overvoltage has its own code, P0C79.

causes.label: Voltage sensing in the power drive unit shorted to supply
Real overvoltage from battery or HV circuit (both motor units report)
Loose or damaged high-voltage connection

symptoms: MIL and hybrid system warning
Electric drive switched off or reduced

P0D31.title: Drive Motor A Inverter Voltage Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0D31.description: P0D31 covers a voltage signal from the drive motor A inverter that drops out or jumps for brief moments without staying out of range long enough for P0D2F or P0D30. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Related checks show the time scale: Mitsubishi rates the same sensor as failed only after 0.16 to 0.3 s outside its window, so shorter glitches need a separate test. Denso describes comparing the measured inverter input voltage with a value estimated from the motor control loop, which also exposes a signal that jitters. Likely triggers are a loose low-voltage connector at the inverter, a chafed harness, or a sensing circuit in the power electronics that fails with heat or vibration. CARB requires such input signals to be checked for circuit faults and rationality. The hybrid warning may come and go.

causes.label: Loose or corroded low-voltage connector at the inverter
Chafed signal wiring with intermittent contact
Sensing circuit in the power electronics fails with heat or vibration

symptoms: Hybrid system warning that comes and goes
Brief power loss or jerky electric drive

P0D32.title: DC/DC Converter A Over Temperature
P0D32.description: P0D32 means DC/DC converter A, which supplies the 12 V network from the high-voltage battery, has become too hot. Unlike the sensor codes P0C38-P0C3C, the reading itself is trusted; the temperature is the problem. Honda names P0D32 in bulletin 26-025 for 2023-2025 Accord Hybrid models alongside other power control unit overheating codes such as P0A3C and P0A3E: road debris can get past a weak guard and damage the PCU radiator, coolant escapes, and several warning lights appear with reduced hybrid performance. The remedy is a new guard and, if the radiator leaks, a new radiator. Low coolant, a weak electronics coolant pump, a clogged radiator or trapped air are the usual causes. The converter cuts or stops its output, so the 12 V battery can run flat.

causes.label: Coolant loss in the power electronics circuit, e.g. damaged PCU radiator (Honda)
Weak electronics coolant pump or air in the cooling circuit
Radiator clogged or airflow restricted
Internal converter fault with excess heat

symptoms: Several warning lights including MIL
Reduced hybrid system performance
12 V battery discharges, charging warning

P0D33.title: DC/DC Converter Current High
P0D33.description: P0D33 says the DC/DC converter carries more current than its limit. The converter links the high-voltage or 48 V system with the 12 V network; an internal short in the power stage, a shorted 12 V cable or consumer, or a failed output stage can push the current beyond what the converter accepts, and it then switches off to protect itself. LKQ Electriq, a high-voltage component remanufacturer, reports P0D33 together with a charging system fault message on Land Rover 48 V mild hybrids (Defender, Evoque, Discovery Sport, Velar); in its bench tests the cause was usually a fault on the converter's internal circuit board, not the vehicle wiring. No manufacturer publishes test limits. The 12 V battery stops being charged and the car may later fail to start. Overheating is P0D32.

causes.label: Internal circuit board fault in the converter (Land Rover MHEV)
Short in a 12 V cable or consumer on the converter output
Damaged high-voltage or 48 V supply cable

symptoms: Charging system fault message
12 V battery not charged, later no start
Electrical consumers switched off

P0D34.title: Hybrid/EV Battery System Current
P0D34.description: P0D34 is the general code for the current flowing through the high-voltage battery system as a whole. The pack current sensor codes P0ABF-P0AC3 judge the sensor signal; this group judges whether the current itself fits the operating state. No manufacturer documents P0D34 publicly, and its set conditions are not published. A plausible reading is a current that does not match what the inverters, the charger and the DC/DC converter should draw, or current flow while the contactors are open. Ford's patent on in-range current sensor faults shows one way to check: amp-hours counted from the measured current are compared with the shift in charge level derived from the open-circuit voltage. CARB requires battery system performance to be monitored. Unstable, low and high current are P0D35, P0D36 and P0D37.

causes.label: Battery current sensor reads wrong but within range
Battery controller software or calibration
Unexpected current path in the HV system (contactor, consumer)

symptoms: Hybrid system warning or MIL
Reduced electric power or charging restrictions

P0D35.title: Hybrid/EV Battery System Current Unstable
P0D35.description: P0D35 flags a battery system current that swings more than the operating state explains, for example rapid changes while the requested power is steady. No manufacturer publishes set conditions for this code. Possible sources are a loose high-voltage connection or a chattering contactor that briefly interrupts the flow, a consumer such as a compressor or heater that cycles abnormally, a current sensor with an intermittent signal, or a controller that oscillates in its regulation. Hitachi Astemo's patent on battery current detection compares several current values and treats a large spread between them as a fault, which illustrates how such instability can be caught. The sensor's own sporadic code is P0AC3; P0D35 concerns the current flow. CARB requires battery system performance monitoring. Power may be cut back.

causes.label: Loose high-voltage connection or chattering contactor
Current sensor or its wiring with intermittent signal
HV consumer (compressor, heater) cycling abnormally

symptoms: Hybrid system warning, possibly intermittent
Power reduction or jerky electric drive

P0D36.title: Hybrid/EV Battery System Current Low
P0D36.description: P0D36 means the battery system delivers or accepts less current than the controller expects for the power it commanded. No manufacturer documents a threshold publicly. Low current can come from high resistance in the high-voltage path, a contactor that does not close properly, an opened fuse in a branch circuit, a pack with high internal resistance, or a sensor that reads too low. The last case is hard to spot: Ford's patent explains that a sensor stuck at a plausible value passes simple range tests and is only found when integrated current is checked against the charge level implied by battery voltage. CARB requires the battery and charging functions to be monitored. Drivers notice weaker electric drive, little regeneration or slow charging. Overcurrent is P0D37; sensor circuit faults are P0AC0-P0AC2.

causes.label: High resistance in the HV path or contactor not closing properly
Current sensor stuck at a plausible but too low value
Aged battery pack with high internal resistance

symptoms: Reduced electric power and regeneration
Slow charging
Hybrid system warning or MIL

P0D37.title: Hybrid/EV Battery System Current High
P0D37.description: P0D37 records excessive current in the high-voltage battery system. Mitsubishi describes it for the 2023 Outlander PHEV: the PHEV-ECU watches the HV circuit for overcurrent whenever the car is ready or charging. Because such a current can damage the contact points of the contactors, the manual requires junction box No. 2 to be replaced, then asks whether the battery controllers, on-board charger, DC/DC converter, A/C unit, power drive unit or rear motor unit store a code, since one of them usually caused the surge; a recurring code within 20 minutes leads to the PHEV-ECU and the drive battery. Mitsubishi shows only the EV system warning, while Ford lists P0D37 with MIL and wrench lamp. Low current is P0D36; a sensor stuck high is P0AC2.

causes.label: Short or fault in an HV component (charger, DC/DC, A/C, inverter)
Contactor points damaged by the overcurrent (junction box)
Damaged high-voltage cable
Hybrid control unit or battery fault (code returns)

symptoms: EV or hybrid system warning, with MIL on some makes
High-voltage system switches off, car not ready or not charging

P0D38.title: Battery Charger A Input Current Sensor Circuit
P0D38.description: P0D38 is the general circuit code for the sensor that measures the AC current entering battery charger A, the on-board charger. It sets when the signal is missing or electrically invalid; range, low, high and intermittent faults have their own codes P0D39-P0D3C. No manufacturer documents P0D38 with set conditions in a public source. Mitsubishi's checks on the sibling codes show the scale: on the 2022 Outlander PHEV a sensor output below 0.344 V or above 4.658 V, about 54 A either way, for 0.5 s stops charging and leads to replacing the combined charger and DC/DC unit. Delta Electronics describes a self-test of a charger's current detection before power flows. Unlike P0D29 and P0D2A, which judge the current itself, P0D38 concerns the measurement. Charging is refused or aborted; driving stays possible.

causes.label: Current sensing inside the on-board charger failed
Open or shorted sensor wiring or connector
Charger software or supply voltage fault

symptoms: AC charging does not start or stops
Charging fault indication on the dashboard or charge port

P0D39.title: Battery Charger A Input Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P0D39.description: P0D39 flags an implausible reading from the sensor that measures alternating current at the input of charger A, the on-board charger. Both documented users test its zero point. GM's charger module in the 2011 Volt sets the code as a Type A fault with MIL when the current value sits 5.4 A or more away from zero for 512 of 640 ms although no current should flow; the 2016 ELR table uses 1.4 A. Mitsubishi's 2022 Outlander PHEV logs it when 1.5 A or more is seen for 2 s while the PHEV-ECU has not released charging, then stops charging and calls for a new charger/DC-DC unit. Hard electrical faults of the same sensor are P0D3A and P0D3B, the general circuit code is P0D38. The car still drives, but AC charging is blocked.

causes.label: Zero point of the current sensor inside the charger has drifted
Measuring electronics of the on-board charger failed
Charger calibration out of date

symptoms: AC charging does not start
MIL on (GM)
Charging fault shown at the charge port or in the cluster

P0D3A.title: Battery Charger A Input Current Sensor Circuit Low
P0D3A.description: P0D3A is the low-signal fault of the charger A input current sensor. Mitsubishi defines it for the 2022 Outlander PHEV as a short to ground: if the sensor output falls below 0.344 V, which corresponds to roughly -54 A, for 0.5 s while the charger supply is 10-16 V, charging is stopped and the combined charger and DC/DC unit is swapped. GM's battery charger control module in the 2011 Volt compares the reported current with a lower bound (0.8 A; 1.65 A in the 2014 table with AC voltage above 80 V) for 160 of 200 ms and rates it Type A, so the MIL comes on. The mirror fault is P0D3B, offset errors fall under P0D39. Usually the sensor inside the charger is at fault rather than outside wiring; charging stays unavailable until repaired.

causes.label: Current sensor signal shorted to ground inside the charger
Failed on-board charger/DC-DC unit
Unstable 12 V supply to the charger module

symptoms: AC charging stops or never begins
MIL on (GM)

P0D3B.title: Battery Charger A Input Current Sensor Circuit High
P0D3B.description: P0D3B reports that the charger A input current sensor reads too high. On the 2022 Outlander PHEV Mitsubishi interprets a sensor voltage above 4.658 V, equivalent to more than about 54 A, lasting 0.5 s as a short to the supply side; charging ends and the integrated charger/DC-DC unit is the listed part. GM's Volt charger module (2011 and 2014 tables) sets the code when the reported AC current exceeds 24.78 A for 160 of 200 ms and lights the MIL as a Type A fault. The low counterpart is P0D3A; a reading that looks valid but carries an offset is P0D39. Since the grid cannot push that much current through the charger unnoticed, the sensor path is the first suspect. Owners see AC charging refuse to start or quit shortly after plugging in.

causes.label: Current sensor signal shorted to supply voltage inside the charger
Failed on-board charger/DC-DC unit
Genuine overcurrent at the charger input from an internal short

symptoms: AC charging quits shortly after plugging in
MIL on (GM)

P0D3C.title: Battery Charger A Input Current Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0D3C.description: P0D3C covers a charger A input current signal that drops out or jumps for short moments instead of staying wrong. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM's Volt and Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV, which use the neighbouring codes P0D39-P0D3B, list no intermittent variant. Under CARB's comprehensive component rules a sensor input must be checked for circuit faults and implausible values, and a sporadic signal is one form of that. Likely triggers are a loose plug or a failing measuring element inside the on-board charger, where Mitsubishi locates the sensor and replaces the whole unit. Because the charger cannot regulate its intake on an unstable current value, charging may stop at random; driving is not affected.

causes.label: Loose or corroded connector at the on-board charger
Current measuring element inside the charger failing
Charger software fault

symptoms: Charging stops at random and may restart
Charge sessions take longer than usual

P0D3D.title: Battery Charger A Input Voltage Sensor A Circuit
P0D3D.description: P0D3D is the basic circuit code for voltage sensor A at the input of charger A, which measures the AC supply voltage arriving from the charge inlet. It stands for a missing or electrically invalid signal; plausibility, low, high and sporadic faults have their own codes P0D3E-P0D41. No manufacturer publishes set conditions for P0D3D itself. GM's Volt charger module and Mitsubishi's 2022 Outlander PHEV only use the detailed siblings; Mitsubishi places the sensor in its combined charger and DC/DC module and stops charging on any of them. CARB requires input components to be checked for circuit continuity, which is what this code expresses. Expect AC charging to be refused while the car remains drivable.

causes.label: Open or shorted voltage sense circuit in the charger
Failed on-board charger
Damaged AC wiring between charge inlet and charger

symptoms: AC charging is refused
Charging fault indication

P0D3E.title: Battery Charger A Input Voltage Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0D3E.description: P0D3E means the AC input voltage seen by the on-board charger does not agree with other information. GM uses it across generations: the 2011-2014 Volt charger module compares the AC peak voltage with two internal bulk voltage readings and sets a Type A fault when both differ by more than 34 V (59 V in 2014); the 2016 and 2019 Volt check the charger's duty-cycle report while driving and fail it outside 8-12 %, Type B. GM bulletins PIC5803B to D tie P0D3E to interrupted charging with certain charging stations and fix it with new BCCM software. Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV flags an input voltage reading of 25 V or more held for 2 s. Electrical low and high faults are P0D3F and P0D40. Usually only charging is affected.

causes.label: Charger module software reacting to certain charging stations (GM BCCM update)
Charging station or cord with unusual behaviour, quick re-plugging
Voltage measurement inside the on-board charger faulty
Faulty duty-cycle signal line between charger and controller (2016-2019 Volt)

symptoms: Charge incomplete or interrupted
MIL on (GM)
Problem appears only at certain charging stations

P0D3F.title: Battery Charger A Input Voltage Sensor A Circuit Low
P0D3F.description: P0D3F reports that the charger's AC input voltage reading is too low. In the 2011-2014 Volt GM's charger module sets it when the AC peak stays below 90 V while AC is present (1.5 s in 2011, 5.5 s in 2014), Type A; the 2016-2019 Volt instead watches a duty-cycle signal at or below 8 %. GM bulletin PIC5803D links it to certain charging stations and to grid brown-outs during storms, 12-08-45-001A to electrical noise on household circuits, and PIT6353 to DC-only NACS adapters plugged into AC chargers on newer GM EVs. Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV treats a sensor output under 0.474 V as a short to ground and stops charging. The opposite fault is P0D40. Check the supply and the charging equipment before replacing parts.

causes.label: Weak, interrupted or noisy AC supply (brown-out, shared circuit)
DC-only adapter used on an AC charger (GM PIT6353)
Charger module software needs update (GM PIC5803D)
Voltage sensor signal shorted to ground in the charger

symptoms: Charging does not start or is interrupted
MIL on (GM)
Charge cord LEDs flash or the charge indicator changes colour repeatedly

P0D40.title: Battery Charger A Input Voltage Sensor A Circuit High
P0D40.description: P0D40 is the high-signal fault of the charger's input voltage sensor. GM's Volt charger module (2011 and 2014 tables) sets it when the measured AC peak exceeds 422 V for 160 of 200 ms and lights the MIL as a Type A fault; in the 2016 and 2019 Volt the controller reads a duty-cycle signal and fails it at 92 % and above or at a constant 0 %, Type B over two trips. Mitsubishi's 2022 Outlander PHEV reads a sensor voltage above 3.161 V, corresponding to more than 492 V, for 0.5 s as a short to power, stops charging and replaces the charger/DC-DC unit. Household and Level 2 supplies do not reach these values, so the sensor path or the signal line is normally to blame. P0D3F is the low counterpart.

causes.label: Voltage sensor signal shorted to supply inside the charger
Open duty-cycle signal line between charger and controller (2016-2019 Volt)
Failed on-board charger

symptoms: AC charging is refused
MIL on (GM)

P0D41.title: Battery Charger A Input Voltage Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0D41.description: P0D41 is reserved for an input voltage sensor A signal at charger A that is intermittent or erratic, i.e. it jumps or drops out briefly. No manufacturer documents this code with set conditions; GM and Mitsubishi only use P0D3E-P0D40 for this sensor. GM's information bulletin 12-08-45-001A shows how unstable household supplies appear in practice: electrical noise on the AC line can disturb charging on the Volt, ELR and Spark EV, sometimes together with P0D3F or P0D3E. CARB's rules for input components cover such signal faults in general. Possible causes are poor contacts between inlet and charger, a degrading sensor in the charger, or a noisy supply. Charging may stop and restart unpredictably; driving continues.

causes.label: Electrical noise or poor grounding on the AC supply
Loose contact between charge inlet and charger
Voltage measurement in the charger degrading

symptoms: Charging stops and restarts unpredictably
Fault appears only at one charging location

P0D42.title: Battery Charger 14 Volt Output Voltage Sensor Circuit
P0D42.description: P0D42 is the circuit code for the sensor that measures voltage at the 14 V output of the battery charger, a low-voltage DC stage built into the on-board charger and distinct from the vehicle's main DC/DC converter. GM's charger module in the Volt and ELR has such an output and monitors its voltage with P0D43-P0D45, yet no manufacturer publishes P0D42 itself. A Ford patent explains the purpose of such a stage: a small converter inside the charger keeps the 12 V bus supplied during charging, so the main contactors and the large converter can stay off. CARB requires circuit checks on inputs of this kind. A fault can leave the 12 V side unsupported while plugged in or interrupt charging; driving is not directly affected.

causes.label: Open or shorted voltage sense circuit of the charger's low-voltage stage
Poor 12 V or ground connection at the charger
Failed on-board charger electronics

symptoms: 12 V battery discharges while the car is plugged in
Charging is interrupted

P0D43.title: Battery Charger 14 Volt Output Voltage Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P0D43.description: P0D43 says the voltage reported for the charger's 14 V output does not fit other measurements of the low-voltage system. GM's battery charger control module in the 2011-2014 Volt and the ELR compares the reading with the run/crank signal voltage and with the voltage of a further enable line (HVEMB); a difference of 6 V or more for 4 of 5 s stores a Type A fault with MIL. The test is suspended while the out-of-range codes P0D44/P0D45 or a reference voltage fault are present. In GM's design this output is a low-voltage DC stage inside the charger, separate from the Volt's accessory power module. A failing sense circuit in the charger is most likely, a poor ground or 12 V feed less so; charging can be affected.

causes.label: Low-voltage sense circuit inside the charger reads wrong
Poor ground or 12 V feed at the charger skews the comparison
Charger module software

symptoms: MIL on (GM)
Charging interrupted or not completed

P0D44.title: Battery Charger 14 Volt Output Voltage Sensor Circuit Low
P0D44.description: P0D44 is logged once the voltage sensor of the charger's 14 V output delivers an implausibly low raw value. In GM's charger module for the 2011-2014 Volt and the ELR the limit is a sensor signal of 1.87 V or less, held for 400 of 500 ms while the low-voltage section is awake; it is a Type A fault and lights the MIL. The 2016 ELR charger table also lists the code as a precondition for its output power checks, and GM's 14 V output power test P0D5B only runs without it. The output is a low-voltage DC stage built into the charger, not the vehicle's primary DC/DC converter. A grounded signal path or failed electronics inside the charger are typical; internal faults are cured only by reprogramming or replacing the charger.

causes.label: Voltage sense signal shorted to ground inside the charger
Failed low-voltage stage of the on-board charger
14 V output collapsed by an external short or overload

symptoms: MIL on (GM)
Charging may stop or not complete

P0D45.title: Battery Charger 14 Volt Output Voltage Sensor Circuit High
P0D45.description: P0D45 is stored when the charger's 14 V output voltage sensor reads too high. GM's battery charger control module in the Volt and ELR fails it at a reading of 16.88 V or above for 400 of 500 ms; the 2011 table rates it Type A, the 2014 table Type B, meaning the MIL comes on only after two consecutive trips. That value lies above the normal regulation band of a 12 V system, so either a genuine overvoltage at the output or a sensor reading stuck high is possible. The low counterpart is P0D44, and the plausibility check P0D43 pauses while either code is active. As with its siblings, the fault sits in the charger's own low-voltage stage rather than in the car's main DC/DC converter.

causes.label: Voltage sense signal shorted to a higher potential inside the charger
Charger low-voltage stage regulating too high
Charger module software

symptoms: MIL on (GM, after two trips in later model years)
Charging may stop

P0D46.title: Battery Charger 14 Volt Output Voltage Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0D46.description: P0D46 stands for a sporadic or unstable signal from the voltage sensor at the 14 V output of the on-board charger. No manufacturer documents it publicly.
