No manufacturer documents P0DD0 publicly, and Ford uses J only for stuck faults. Toshiba patent US20130026994A1 describes one way to spot a broken link: a small current source parallel to the balancing switch lets the chip compare the sense pin with the balancing pin and flag an open terminal. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 asks for separate fault codes that point to the smallest replaceable part. Stuck and plausibility faults of J use P0DD1 to P0DD3.

causes.label: Open balancing or sense terminal of group J (lead, crimp or weld)
Loose or corroded connector between group J and its monitoring board
Faulty monitoring chip channel serving circuit J

symptoms: Hybrid battery warning with check engine light
Charging or electric drive limited by the battery controller

P0DD1.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit J Stuck On
P0DD1.description: P0DD1: group J's bleed path keeps drawing current after balancing should have ended. Ford's 2014 OBD summary for its hybrids and plug-ins assigns the code to the BECM, which checks at power-up, before the contactors close, for 100 ms: if one of the six cells in the circuit sits more than 75 mV away from the mean of all cells, and this repeats on two consecutive power cycles, the fault is stored. Ford's 2014 code list marks it as a MIL code. Designers guard against this failure: LaunchPoint patent US8598840B2 lets current flow through a bleed resistor only with an encoded, redundant enable that a timer cancels if it is not withdrawn. Group J will sag during standstill. Opposite case: P0DD2.

causes.label: Balancing transistor of group J shorted and conducting permanently
Balancing enable for channel J not withdrawn by the monitoring electronics
Cell in group J with high self-discharge producing the same voltage pattern

symptoms: Check engine light and hybrid battery warning after switching on
Group J clearly lower than the rest after parking
Shorter electric range

P0DD2.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit J Stuck Off
P0DD2.description: P0DD2 marks circuit J as unable to bleed: balancing is commanded, but the six cells of group J keep their charge. Ford lists the code in its 2015 hybrid OBD summary with the same power-up test as for the stuck-on case, run for 100 ms with the contactors still open, two consecutive power cycles and the 75 mV limit against the average cell voltage. GM's 2013 eAssist table documents a more direct test under its own code P1EAA: with the key off and the contactors open, a cell's balancing resistor is switched on and the cell voltage has to move by at least 0.1 V; two failed samples across key cycles give a Type A fault. Over many charges group J ends up high and caps the full charge. Opposite: P0DD1.

causes.label: Bleed resistor of circuit J open or burnt
Balancing switch of group J no longer closing
Interrupted balancing lead between cell tap and board

symptoms: Check engine light without noticeable change in driving
Cells of group J at the top of the cell list at the end of charging
Usable battery capacity declining over time

P0DD3.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit J Range/Performance
P0DD3.description: P0DD3 is a plausibility verdict on circuit J: the switch reacts, but the effect of balancing on group J does not match what the controller expected. No maker documents this code publicly, so the reasoning rests on CARB and on how balancing is planned. Ford patent US20120293129A1 describes active balancing in which the highest cell is discharged for a time that depends on its charge gap to the lowest cell, and the removed charge is moved back into the pack. A gap that stays after such a run, or a run that ends too soon, points to wrong estimates or a weak path rather than an open circuit. 13 CCR 1968.2 requires detection once balancing can no longer hold desired cell voltages. Electrical faults of J: P0DD0.

causes.label: Wrong charge estimate for the cells of group J
Battery controller software or calibration (check for updates first)
Balancing path of J with raised resistance, so less charge moves than planned

symptoms: Check engine light, often only after several charges
Group J remains out of line despite balancing
Unsteady range prediction

P0DD4.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit K
P0DD4.description: P0DD4 is the electrical fault code for balancing circuit K, the eleventh group, so it only exists on packs with at least eleven balancing channels. Public maker documents for this exact code were not found; Ford's summaries give K only to the stuck faults P0DD5 and P0DD6. How a monitoring chip catches broken wiring is shown in Infineon's TLE9012DQU data sheet: during its round-robin cycle the chip sinks a test current of about 15 mA into each balancing pin, odd channels in one cycle and even ones in the next, and flags a broken wire or missing load when the resulting change in cell voltage falls outside a set window. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 requires such components to be monitored on hybrids. Related: P0DD5 to P0DD7.

causes.label: Open wire or loose cell tap in group K
Corrosion or moisture at the connector of the monitoring board for K
Defective monitoring chip or external balancing part of channel K

symptoms: Check engine light and hybrid system warning
Missing or implausible cell voltages for group K in the scan tool
Reduced charging or drive power

P0DD5.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit K Stuck On
P0DD5.description: P0DD5 tells that circuit K is discharging its cells without a balancing request. Ford's 2016 hybrid OBD summary links the code to the BECM start-up check: before the contactors close it looks at the six cells of the circuit for 100 ms and fails it when one of them is more than 75 mV away from the average, confirmed on a second power cycle. A switch that conducts by itself can also be caught directly: in Toshiba patent US20130026994A1 the balancing switch is held off while a comparator watches the nodes on both sides of it; if one side sinks below the other, the switch is judged short-circuited. Apart from charge loss, the shorted path heats its resistor all the time. Inactive case: P0DD6.

causes.label: Shorted balancing switch of group K
Heat damage or contamination bridging the balancing path of K on the board
Driver stage of the monitoring chip holding channel K on

symptoms: Check engine light at start-up
Group K drops faster than the other cells while parked
Locally higher battery module temperature

P0DD6.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit K Stuck Off
P0DD6.description: P0DD6: group K's bleed path stays dead when balancing is called for. Ford includes it in its 2017 hybrid OBD summary; the BECM decides at power-up with open contactors, within 100 ms and over two power cycles, using the 75 mV deviation of one of the six cells from the average. LG's patent US20110285539A1 offers a direct check of the path: a sampling capacitor first takes on the cell's voltage and is then emptied through the balancing circuit; whatever voltage is left over must be close to zero, otherwise the circuit is faulty. Because nothing is drained, the car drives normally, but group K keeps reaching full charge first and the pack loses usable capacity. The stuck-on counterpart is P0DD5.

causes.label: Open bleed resistor in circuit K
Balancing switch of group K failing to turn on
Cracked solder joint in the balancing path of K

symptoms: Check engine light while the car drives normally
Group K highest at the end of charging
Electric range decreasing over many charges

P0DD7.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit K Range/Performance
P0DD7.description: P0DD7 points to balancing of group K that works, but not within the expected limits. No maker publishes this code. A monitoring chip can deliver exactly this kind of finding: Infineon's TLE9012DQU checks every channel during active balancing for overcurrent and undercurrent through a sense resistor and switches balancing off when either threshold is crossed. Its per-cell timer runs up to roughly 3.9 hours in steps of about 7.5 minutes. A current that is too low over such a period moves far less charge than planned, so group K stays apart without any open or shorted part. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 accepts checking the commanded switches as long as the system notices that desired cell voltages are no longer held. Electrical fault: P0DD4.

causes.label: Balancing current of K below the expected value (aged resistor, raised contact resistance)
Controller calibration with too short balancing time for group K
A cell in group K drifting faster than balancing can compensate

symptoms: Check engine light, often after charging
Spread of group K returns soon after a balancing session
Fluctuating range estimate

P0DD8.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit L
P0DD8.description: P0DD8 concerns the hardware of balancing circuit L, the twelfth group. No manufacturer documents it publicly; Ford, whose hybrid BECM runs through letter N, uses L only in the stuck codes P0DD9 and P0DDA. LG Chem's patent EP2730933A1 shows a way to test one balancing circuit through its neighbour: diagnosis resistors sit between each balancing circuit and its cell terminals, and when the circuit under test is switched on or off, the voltage measured across the adjacent circuit has to change in a known pattern. A missing or wrong pattern exposes a broken resistor, switch or connection. The CARB regulation requires separate codes that lead the technician to the replaceable unit. Stuck and plausibility faults of L: P0DD9 to P0DDB.

causes.label: Open resistor, switch or solder joint in circuit L
Poor connection of the cell taps of group L
Faulty voltage measuring channel next to circuit L

symptoms: Hybrid battery warning and check engine light
Power or charging limited

P0DD9.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit L Stuck On
P0DD9.description: P0DD9: the balancing path of group L will not switch off. The 2018 edition of Ford's hybrid OBD summary contains the code; the BECM catches it at power-up with the contactors still open, in a 100 ms check that compares each of the six cells of circuit L with the average and fails above 75 mV, again over two power cycles. GM shows a different route in its 2013 eAssist table: code P1B33 compares the reported balancing switch status with the commanded one and fails after 7 of 10 samples, as a two-trip fault. A switch that reads on while it should be off is exactly what P0DD9 describes. While parked the group drains, and the warm resistor stresses the module. Inactive opposite: P0DDA.

causes.label: Balancing switch of group L shorted
Switch status feedback of channel L reporting on although the switch is open
Balancing command for L not cleared by the monitoring electronics

symptoms: Check engine light after switching on
Group L lower than the others after standing
Less electric range

P0DDA.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit L Stuck Off
P0DDA.description: P0DDA says circuit L does not discharge when it is told to. In Ford's 2019 hybrid OBD summary the start-up test has been simplified: it still runs for 100 ms before the contactors close, but the requirement of two consecutive power cycles is gone, and the 75 mV deviation of a cell from the average must instead persist for 0.1 s. Ford's 2014 code list flags the code for the MIL. Renesas patent US9735567B2 explains why a switch that never closes can be seen electrically: a pull-up lifts the balancing pin to cell potential, so a switch that is told to close while the pin still shows the full cell voltage means the path is open. Group L then lags behind in every balancing run and limits the charge. Opposite case: P0DD9.

causes.label: Balancing switch of group L stays open when commanded on
Bleed resistor of circuit L open
Missing gate drive for the balancing switch of L

symptoms: Check engine light with no change in drivability
Group L reaches full charge before the rest
Gradual loss of usable capacity

P0DDB.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit L Range/Performance
P0DDB.description: P0DDB stands for balancing of group L whose result is out of range although the circuit answers. No maker documents P0DDB publicly. A patent by Southwest Electronic Energy, US9097774B2, adds an important angle: it counts how often each cell has to be balanced and flags a cell that needs it far more or less often than the others, since an internal short can be the reason. Applied here, a plausibility fault of L may not be a balancing defect at all but a cell that keeps losing charge. That makes a careful look at self-discharge and cell voltages worthwhile before parts are replaced. CARB requires hybrids to flag a balancing system that fails to keep cells at their target voltage. Electrical fault of L: P0DD8.

causes.label: Cell in group L with an internal soft short, needing balancing again and again
Controller calibration of expected balancing effect for L
Drifted bleed resistor of circuit L

symptoms: Check engine light, sometimes only after long parking
Group L drifting low between charges
Range estimate varying from day to day

P0DDC.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit M
P0DDC.description: P0DDC reports an electrical fault of balancing circuit M, the thirteenth group, which only large packs with at least thirteen channels possess. No maker publishes this exact code; in Ford's BECM documents M appears only as stuck on (P0DDD) and stuck off (P0DDE). LaunchPoint's patent US8598840B2 describes how such faults can be found while the system runs: built-in tests feed every cell measurement its own distinct test signal and are run from a circuit domain kept separate from the balancing and measuring electronics they check, so one failure cannot hide itself. Wiring breaks, damaged connectors and chip faults are typical findings. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 requires these parts to be watched on hybrids. Related: P0DDD to P0DDF.

causes.label: Broken sense or balancing wire of group M
Damaged or poorly seated connector at the board for M
Fault in the monitoring electronics of channel M

symptoms: Check engine light and hybrid warning
Battery controller restricting power or charging

P0DDD.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit M Stuck On
P0DDD.description: P0DDD reports a balancing path of group M that keeps conducting. Ford's 2015 hybrid OBD summary places it in the BECM monitor, judged at power-up before the contactors close: 100 ms, six cells per circuit, more than 75 mV from the average, two consecutive power cycles. A properly working chip should never leave a channel on indefinitely. Infineon's TLE9012DQU, for example, gives each cell its own balancing timer of up to about 3.9 hours and ends balancing on its own once that runs out, or when its over- or undercurrent check trips. If group M still loses charge after such limits, the switch itself is most likely shorted. Expect a low group M after a night of parking. Inactive counterpart: P0DDE.

causes.label: Shorted balancing switch of group M that no timer can stop
Damaged external balancing transistor on the board for M
High self-discharge cell in group M imitating a stuck switch

symptoms: Check engine light at start-up
Group M noticeably low after overnight parking
Raised module temperature near group M

P0DDE.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit M Stuck Off
P0DDE.description: P0DDE means group M is not bled when it should be. Ford carries the code in its 2016 hybrid OBD summary with the usual BECM start-up rule: 100 ms with open contactors, six cells per circuit, a 75 mV gap to the average, confirmed over two power cycles. A balancing channel can also be stopped on purpose, which a diagnosis must keep apart from a real failure. TI's BQ79616-Q1 data sheet lists such ends: the per-channel timer expires, the cell falls below a set voltage, an unmasked fault appears or the host stops balancing. Only a path that never conducts after a valid start counts here. Left alone, the fuller cells of M reach their limit first at every charge, and the pack gives away capacity. Stuck-on case: P0DDD.

causes.label: Bleed resistor of circuit M open
Balancing switch of group M that no longer turns on
Intended balancing stop for M misjudged as no response by the software

symptoms: Check engine light while driving feels normal
Group M highest at the end of each charge
Less usable battery energy over time

P0DDF.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit M Range/Performance
P0DDF.description: P0DDF covers group M when balancing responds but its outcome is not credible. No manufacturer publishes this code. Ford patent US9145064B2 shows what the expected outcome can be built on: the controller derives a bleed time per cell from that cell's surplus capacity and the charging current, so that all cells arrive at the target together at the end of charging. If group M is still out of line once its time is used up, the plan or the hardware behind it is off. Typical reasons are a capacity estimate that no longer matches an aged cell or a resistor that has drifted. The CARB hybrid rule in 13 CCR 1968.2 calls for exactly this functional check. Electrical fault of M: P0DDC.

causes.label: Stored capacity value for cells of group M out of date
Battery controller software (update before repair)
Bleed resistor of M drifted

symptoms: Check engine light following charging sessions
Group M not aligned with the rest after full charge
Inconsistent range display

P0DE0.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit N
P0DE0.description: P0DE0 flags a wiring or driver fault in balancing circuit N, the fourteenth and last letter of the series; the next code, P0DE4, belongs to a different system. Packs with more balancing groups than fourteen must therefore map several groups to one letter or use their own codes. Ford's hybrid BECM is one of the few documented users that fills all fourteen letters, but only with stuck codes, so P0DE0 itself has no public maker source. How a broken balancing terminal is found is shown in Toshiba patent US20130026994A1, where comparing the sense pin with the balancing pin reveals an open connection. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 requires codes that point to the smallest replaceable unit. Stuck and plausibility faults of N: P0DE1 to P0DE3.

causes.label: Open balancing terminal or lead of group N
Corroded or loose connector at the last module board
Monitoring chip channel for N defective

symptoms: Hybrid battery warning with check engine light
Electric operation or charging restricted

P0DE1.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit N Stuck On
P0DE1.description: P0DE1 is the last stuck-on code of the series: group N keeps bleeding when it should rest. Ford lists it in every hybrid OBD summary from 2014 to 2019; in the 2017 edition the BECM spends 100 ms after key-on, while the contactors are still open, checking whether any of the six cells of circuit N sits more than 75 mV from the average, with two consecutive power cycles needed. A balancing switch that cannot open drains the group constantly, even with the car parked, and turns that energy into heat on the board. A cell with an internal short can produce the same falling voltage, so a check of the switch on the bench is worthwhile before the cells are condemned. Ford's 2014 code list ties the code to the MIL. Inactive case: P0DE2.

causes.label: Balancing switch of group N permanently conducting
Cell of group N with an internal short causing the same voltage drop
Monitoring electronics keeping the balancing command for N active

symptoms: Check engine light after switching on
Group N drops while the car is parked
Shorter electric range

P0DE2.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit N Stuck Off
P0DE2.description: P0DE2 closes Ford's list of balancing codes: circuit N does not discharge when commanded. Ford's 2018 hybrid summary has the BECM judge this during a 100 ms window at key-on, contactors still open, comparing each of the six cells with the average against 75 mV over two power cycles. A switch that stays open has no immediate effect on driving, but the imbalance adds up. Intersil's application note AN141 puts numbers on this: cells count as matched when their capacities lie within 3 percent, and a gap of only 150 mV at full charge can cost a series pack a quarter of its capacity or more. Group N will therefore be full first and limit what the whole pack can store. Stuck-on counterpart: P0DE1.

causes.label: Open bleed resistor in circuit N
Balancing switch of group N not turning on
Cell tap of group N detached from the busbar

symptoms: Check engine light without driving complaint
Charging ends early because group N is full first
Electric range shrinking over months

P0DE3.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit N Range/Performance
P0DE3.description: P0DE3 is the final code of the balancing series and judges whether balancing of group N achieves a believable result. No maker documents it publicly. The Wikipedia article on battery balancing explains why such a check matters: unless the upper and lower cut-offs line up with the weakest cell, the energy the pack can take in and give back stays limited, so a mismatched group throttles the whole battery. Passive systems burn the surplus in resistors, active ones move it over to the emptier cells. If group N stays apart although its circuit reacts, the cause lies in estimates, cell ageing or a weak bleed path. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 obliges hybrid monitors to catch cells drifting away from their balancing target. Electrical fault: P0DE0.

causes.label: Cells of group N aged unevenly
Controller estimates or calibration for group N off
Bleed path of N with too little current

symptoms: Check engine light, mostly after charging
Group N never quite levels with the other groups
Reduced and unsteady range

P0DE4.title: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Motor Over Temperature
P0DE4.description: P0DE4 reports that the electric motor of auxiliary transmission fluid pump A has run too hot. Such a pump keeps the transmission pressurised while the engine is stopped, either by start-stop or during electric driving in a hybrid. No manufacturer documents P0DE4 publicly. Ford's 2019 hybrid OBD summary shows how its plug-in hybrids treat pump heat under other codes: once the pump circuit board exceeds 130 °C for 3 s the TCM logs P175A and disables the pump, and above 135 °C the event feeds the stall code P0C2A. Heat builds when the motor labours against low, aged or very cold fluid, against a binding rotor, or in a hot transmission. The car then usually keeps the engine running instead of stopping or driving electrically. P0C1B is the controller electronics, P277D the motor of pump B.

causes.label: Low, aged or wrong transmission fluid making the pump work harder
Binding rotor or worn bearing in the pump motor
Transmission running hot (towing, heat, restricted fluid cooler)
Faulty temperature evaluation in the pump controller or outdated software

symptoms: Start-stop no longer shuts the engine off
Electric driving limited, engine keeps running
Harsh engagement when pulling away after a stop
Malfunction indicator lamp on

P0DE5.title: Charge Status Indicator B Control Circuit/Open
P0DE5.description: P0DE5 flags an interrupted drive circuit for charge status indicator B, a second lamp or LED that tells the owner whether the vehicle is charging, for instance one at the charge port next to the one on the dashboard. Which light gets the letter B is up to the maker. No manufacturer documents P0DE5 publicly. GM's tables for the Chevrolet Volt and Cadillac ELR only cover indicator A (P0D2C): the hybrid controller samples the LED driver every 100 ms, needs 40 bad results out of 50 and checks for a short to battery or an open line while the LED is commanded off. In the current code set, shorts on B have their own codes, P0E41 and P0E42, so P0DE5 narrows the fault to a break: a cut wire, a loose connector or a dead LED. Charging itself still works.

causes.label: Broken wire or unplugged connector to indicator B
Burnt-out LED or failed indicator unit
Corroded contacts in the weather-exposed charge port area
Failed output driver in the controlling module

symptoms: Charge status indicator B stays dark while charging
Charging works normally
Warning lamp possible depending on the manufacturer

P0DE6.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cell Voltage Low
P0DE6.description: P0DE6 means the battery controller has measured at least one cell of the high-voltage pack below its lower voltage limit. It concerns a real reading, not the sensing lines (P0B3D and similar), and it looks at the weakest cell rather than the charge of the whole pack (P0A7D). Ford pairs it with P0A7D on 2020 Escape and Explorer hybrids drained by long standing or failed starts; a rescue charge needs the lowest cell above 1.45 V and a cell spread under 2.5 V (SSM 49163, later 51460, 52230 and 52773 for 2023-24 models). Stellantis fixes P0DE6 with BPCM software on the 2024-25 Dodge Charger EV and Jeep Wagoneer S, and on the 2026 Cherokee hybrid lengthened its maturing time for cold cranks. A no-start or reduced power is typical.

causes.label: Pack deeply discharged after long standing or repeated failed starts
Battery controller software judging too strictly (e.g. cold cranking)
Single weak cell with high self-discharge or lost capacity
Cell balancing circuit draining one cell

symptoms: Vehicle will not start or switch to ready
Reduced power, no electric driving
Malfunction indicator lamp on

P0DE7.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cell Voltage High
P0DE7.description: P0DE7 is stored when a single cell of the high-voltage pack climbs above the upper voltage limit the battery controller permits. Overcharged lithium-ion cells age quickly and can become unsafe, so the controller usually restricts charging and regenerative braking until the cell is back in range. The only public manufacturer use found is Ram: bulletin 08-030-24 and its sister bulletins for the 2019-2024 Ram 1500 with eTorque mild hybrid (3.6 L V6 and 5.7 L V8) list P0DE7 together with cell supervisory, voltage sense and balancing codes and prescribe new BPCM software, pointing to a calibration cause. Other plausible causes are failed balancing, a cell with raised internal resistance during regen, or a drifting measurement chip. Low cell voltage is P0DE6, pack overvoltage P0AFB.

causes.label: Battery controller software or calibration (documented by Ram)
Cell balancing no longer bleeding off the highest cell
Aged cell with raised internal resistance overshooting during regen
Drifting cell monitoring chip reporting too high a value

symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Weaker regenerative braking, charging limited
Mild-hybrid assist or start-stop unavailable

P0DE8.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve C Control Circuit/Open
P0DE8.description: P0DE8 reports an open or otherwise faulty drive circuit for coolant control valve C, a third switchable valve in the coolant loop of the hybrid or EV battery. What it switches depends on the layout, for example whether coolant passes through the radiator, the air-conditioning chiller or a heater, and the maker decides which valve is called C. No manufacturer documents P0DE8 publicly. The closest documented case is valve A: the battery management of Mercedes S-, E- and C-Class hybrids flags its actuation as electrically faulty or open with P0CDF00 (LI83.30-P-061224). CARB demands circuit checks on every output used to heat or cool the energy store. Expect a broken wire, a loose plug or an open coil. Shorts are P0DEB and P0DEC, an overloaded driver P0E22.

causes.label: Broken wire or loose connector at valve C
Open coil or motor winding inside valve C
Corroded pins from coolant or water ingress
Failed driver stage in the controlling module

symptoms: Battery temperature control works only in a fallback mode
Charging or drive power reduced when the pack is too hot or cold
Malfunction indicator lamp on

P0DE9.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve C Performance/Stuck Off
P0DE9.description: P0DE9 says coolant control valve C is electrically fine but does not do its job: it fails to reach the commanded position or remains in its off state. No manufacturer documents P0DE9 publicly. GM's 2011 Chevrolet Volt tables show what such a test can look like for valve A, which has a position feedback: on start-up the valve must find its end stop within 800 ms, later it must reach each target within 1.5 s, and an erratic feedback with more than 12 % noise counts as well; enough failed samples set a Type B code with the MIL on the second trip. Where no feedback exists, makers judge the valve from coolant or pack temperatures, which CARB requests as a functional check of cooling. Dirt, a seized valve body or a weak actuator are typical. Stuck on is P0DEA.

causes.label: Valve body seized or sluggish from deposits
Worn actuator motor or gearing in valve C
Low coolant or air in the battery loop distorting the temperature check
Overly tight diagnostic calibration

symptoms: Battery heats up faster under load or while fast charging
Charging power or drive power limited
Malfunction indicator lamp on

P0DEA.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve C Stuck On
P0DEA.description: P0DEA means coolant control valve C stays in its active position even though the controller has asked it to return. A wiring check cannot see this, because the circuit is intact; the controller needs a position feedback, as on GM's Volt valve with its own sensor codes, or it infers the state from coolant and pack temperatures that keep moving the wrong way. No manufacturer documents P0DEA publicly. Mercedes battery management shows for valve A that the same mechanical fault can be named in both directions, with separate codes for a shutoff valve that will not close and one that will not open (P0CE000, P0CE100). Depending on what C controls, coolant keeps flowing through the chiller or heater path, so the pack may be overcooled in winter or kept warm in summer. Stuck off is P0DE9.

causes.label: Valve jammed in the active position by debris or wear
Driver stage that does not switch off
Software misreading the temperature response

symptoms: Pack too cold in winter or too warm in summer
Reduced range or charging speed
Malfunction indicator lamp on

P0DEB.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve C Control Circuit Low
P0DEB.description: P0DEB is set when the drive line of coolant control valve C reads too low, which almost always means a short to ground somewhere between controller and valve. No manufacturer documents P0DEB publicly. GM's 2011 Volt tables for valve A show the logic: with system voltage above 9 V, a low reading on driver line 1 during reverse travel counts as a failure, and 90 failures out of 100 samples at 6.25 ms set a Type B code. A short to ground lets current bypass the load, so many drivers protect themselves by shutting off; an overheated or overloaded driver has its own code, P0E22. Chafed insulation near brackets, coolant in the connector and an internal short in the valve motor are the usual finds. The valve then stays wherever it was. Open circuit is P0DE8, short to voltage P0DEC.

causes.label: Chafed wire shorting to body ground
Coolant or water in the valve connector
Internal short in the valve motor

symptoms: Valve C no longer moves, temperature control in fallback mode
Charging or drive power reduced at temperature extremes
Malfunction indicator lamp on

P0DEC.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve C Control Circuit High
P0DEC.description: P0DEC is the short-to-voltage case for coolant control valve C: its drive line reads high at a moment when the controller expects it low. No manufacturer documents P0DEC publicly. For valve A, GM's 2011 Volt checks driver line 1 for a high level while the valve should be stopped or moving forward, again needing 90 failures in 100 checks for a Type B code. Unlike a ground short, a line held at supply voltage can keep the valve energised, so the valve may creep to an end stop instead of freezing. Keep the drive circuit apart from the feedback: on valves with a position sensor, a signal above the valid range is a sensor code such as P0CE7, not P0DEC. A wire pinched against a live feed or a driver that will not switch off is typical. Short to ground is P0DEB, open circuit P0DE8.

causes.label: Wire pinched against a supply line
Driver stage in the module not switching off
Moisture bridging pins in the connector

symptoms: Valve C runs to an end position and stays there
Pack temperature drifts, power or charging limited
Malfunction indicator lamp on

P0DED.title: Pedestrian Alert Control Module Circuit/Open
P0DED.description: P0DED points to an open or faulty hard-wired circuit between the powertrain side and the pedestrian alert control module, the unit that makes a quiet hybrid or EV audible at low speed. It is not a network fault, which is U013F, nor a speaker fault, which uses B0122 and B0123. No manufacturer documents P0DED publicly. The module exists because of law: US standard FMVSS 141 requires a sound whenever propulsion is active and the car is not in Park, in reverse and up to about 30 km/h, and the EU has demanded such a system for new types since July 2019. Ford calls the unit PACM; on the 2020-21 Escape Hybrid it sits in the right rear quarter (TSB 21-2271). An open line typically means a silent car, so pedestrians lose their warning and the driver usually sees a message.

causes.label: Broken wire or loose connector at the alert module
Blown fuse or interrupted supply to the module
Internal fault of the pedestrian alert module

symptoms: No artificial driving sound at low speed or in reverse
Pedestrian alert warning message in the instrument cluster

P0DEE.title: Pedestrian Alert Control Module Circuit Low
P0DEE.description: P0DEE is set when the hard-wired circuit to the pedestrian alert control module sits below its expected voltage, typically from a short to ground. No manufacturer documents P0DEE publicly, so the exact signal behind it, whether supply, wake-up or a command line, is not known in detail. A ground short often blows a fuse or makes the driving module disconnect the line, and the alert then falls silent, even though FMVSS 141 expects a sound from standstill with propulsion on, in reverse and up to around 30 km/h; EU vehicles must carry such a system as well. Look along the whole harness run, which can be long: on Ford's 2020-21 Escape Hybrid the module sits in the right rear quarter. Open circuit is P0DED, short to voltage P0DEF.

causes.label: Chafed or crushed wire shorting to ground
Water ingress in a connector near bumper or wheel arch
Internal short in the alert module

symptoms: Pedestrian warning sound missing
Warning message in the instrument cluster
Fuse for the alert module may be blown

P0DEF.title: Pedestrian Alert Control Module Circuit High
P0DEF.description: P0DEF reports a voltage above the permitted window on the wired link to the pedestrian alert control module, most often because a wire touches a supply line or the line has lost its ground reference. No manufacturer documents P0DEF publicly. The consequence differs from the low case: a line stuck high may leave the module permanently woken or commanded, so instead of silence the alert can behave oddly, for example sounding when it should not or draining the 12 V battery while parked. Whether that happens depends on the design. The legal background is the same as for the siblings: FMVSS 141 and the EU require a warning sound for quiet vehicles at low speed. Ford names the unit PACM. P0DED is an open circuit, P0DEE a short to ground, U013F lost communication.

causes.label: Wire pinched against a 12 V supply line
Loose or corroded ground connection of the module
Internal fault of the alert module or its driver

symptoms: Pedestrian sound missing or sounding at the wrong time
Warning message in the instrument cluster
Possible 12 V battery drain while parked

P0DF0.title: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit
P0DF0.description: P0DF0 is the catch-all circuit code for temperature sensor B in the generator inverter, the power stage that drives the generator of a two-machine hybrid. The controller sets it when the sensor line is electrically faulty but the fault is not sorted into low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents P0DF0 publicly. Mitsubishi fits one thermistor per IGBT in the generator unit of the Outlander PHEV and reports the second high-side sensor (V phase) only through P0DF4 to P0DF6, never through this general code; Ford likewise names only open and short checks for its generator inverter sensor. CARB requires every input that feeds inverter thermal management to be checked for circuit faults. Without a valid value the controller has to assume the worst and usually limits generator output.

causes.label: Loose, corroded or damaged connector at the inverter or power unit
Thermistor or its signal path inside the inverter module faulty
Faulty evaluation input in the generator control unit

symptoms: Hybrid or engine warning light on
Reduced generator output, weaker charging while driving
Hybrid system may switch to a restricted mode

P0DF1.title: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0DF1.description: P0DF1 means the signal of generator inverter temperature sensor B drops out or jumps for short moments and then looks normal again. Typical triggers are temperature steps faster than the power module could physically heat or cool, or brief readings that resemble an open line. No manufacturer documents P0DF1 publicly: Ford's monitors for its generator inverter sensor cover only opens and shorts (P0BCE, P0BCF), and Mitsubishi has no intermittent code for the corresponding V-phase sensor at all. CARB still expects inverter thermal inputs to be monitored. Because the fault comes and goes, freeze frame data and a wiggle test of the inverter harness tell more than swapping parts. A steady fault on this sensor would be logged as P0DF0, P0DF5 or P0DF6 instead.

causes.label: Loose or fretted terminal in the inverter connector
Harness chafing or vibration damage near the power unit
Intermittent contact inside the inverter module

symptoms: Warning light that comes and goes
Occasional short loss of generator power
Fault often not reproducible at the workshop

P0DF2.title: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor C Circuit
P0DF2.description: P0DF2 covers an electrical fault on temperature sensor C of the generator inverter that the controller cannot assign to a more specific low, high or intermittent code. Which power switch carries sensor C is up to the manufacturer; in Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV the third high-side IGBT sensor sits on the W phase, and its faults are logged only as P0DF7 to P0DF9. No manufacturer documents P0DF2 itself. CARB demands circuit monitoring for inputs of inverter thermal management. As these thermistors are usually built into the IGBT module, a confirmed sensor fault often means replacing the inverter or the complete power unit, so the harness and connector deserve a careful check first. The general circuit code for sensor B is P0DF0.

causes.label: Thermistor inside the IGBT module defective
Connector or signal line fault between module and controller
Faulty input stage in the generator control unit

symptoms: Hybrid or engine warning light on
Generator power reduced as a precaution
Higher engine use or weaker battery recharge

P0DF3.title: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor C Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0DF3.description: P0DF3 is logged when sensor C in the generator inverter delivers an unsteady signal: short spikes, gaps or values that change faster than the module temperature ever could. Such faults often start at connectors that loosen under engine vibration and repeated heating cycles, or at pins attacked by moisture. No manufacturer documents P0DF3 publicly, and Mitsubishi, which does monitor a W-phase sensor in its generator unit, defines no intermittent code for it. CARB requires these thermal inputs to be monitored nonetheless. The warning may vanish after a restart and return days later, so it pays to note when and under which load it appeared. Constant faults of the same sensor are P0DF2, P0DF8 and P0DF9; the matching fault on sensor B is P0DF1.

causes.label: Terminal losing contact under vibration or heat cycles
Moisture or corrosion in the inverter connector
Intermittent connection inside the inverter module

symptoms: Warning light that appears only now and then
Brief drops in generator power
Code stored as history fault without current symptoms

P0DF4.title: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P0DF4.description: P0DF4 reports that temperature sensor B of the generator inverter delivers an electrically valid signal whose value does not fit the other sensors. Mitsubishi documents the check for the Outlander PHEV: a single time in each drive cycle, following at least 600 s of standstill and with the IGBTs switched off, the V-phase high-side sensor may not differ by more than 47 °C from the other two phase sensors for 0.1 s; otherwise P0DF4-00 is stored and the power drive unit is replaced. Volvo lists ECM P0DF400 for 2022-on T8 plug-in hybrids and warns it can be misdetected, showing Propulsion System Service Required; for builds from week 202147 to 202446 ECM software 3.4.4 cures it. Out-of-range signals are P0DF5 and P0DF6.

causes.label: Control software misdetection (Volvo T8, ECM update available)
Sensor in the power module drifted or stuck at one value
Internal fault in the power drive unit (Mitsubishi replaces the unit)

symptoms: Message such as Propulsion System Service Required
Engine warning light on
Turtle symbol and reduced power in some cases

P0DF5.title: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low
P0DF5.description: P0DF5 sets when the signal voltage of generator inverter temperature sensor B stays below its valid window. Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV checks this continuously: if the V-phase high-side IGBT sensor reads at most 1.25 V during 0.08 s while the generator control unit has at least 8 V supply, P0DF5-00 is stored. Mitsubishi does not say which temperature this means, but with a thermistor whose resistance falls as it warms, a low voltage looks like an extremely hot switch, the usual picture of a short to ground or a shorted element. The guided repair ends with a new power drive unit because the sensor is internal. Expect reduced generator power while the fault is present. The high case is P0DF6, an implausible in-range value P0DF4.

causes.label: Signal line shorted to ground
Shorted thermistor inside the IGBT module
Internal fault of the power drive unit

symptoms: Engine or hybrid warning light on
Generator output limited, engine runs more often
Displayed inverter temperature implausibly high

P0DF6.title: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit High
P0DF6.description: P0DF6 is the high-signal case for sensor B in the generator inverter. In the Outlander PHEV Mitsubishi stores P0DF6-00 when the V-phase high-side IGBT sensor voltage reaches at least 3.75 V during 0.08 s, again only with a GCU supply of at least 8 V. A voltage at the upper limit mostly points to an interrupted sensor line, a lost reference ground or a cracked element; with the common NTC layout it reads as an implausibly cold module. Since the inverter can then no longer protect its switches against overheating, the controller works with a safe substitute and may cut generator output. Mitsubishi's procedure ends with a new power drive unit. Too low a signal on this sensor is P0DF5; the same open-type fault on sensor C would be P0DF9.

causes.label: Open signal line or backed-out terminal
Lost sensor reference ground
Cracked sensor element or internal fault of the power drive unit

symptoms: Engine or hybrid warning light on
Inverter temperature shown far too low
Generator power reduced

P0DF7.title: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
P0DF7.description: P0DF7 is the plausibility code for temperature sensor C of the generator inverter. The idea behind it: after a long rest every power switch should be at roughly the same temperature, so a sensor that stands out is suspect. In Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV the W-phase high-side sensor is compared once per trip, after 600 s or more of soak and with the IGBTs off, against the U- and V-phase sensors; a gap above 47 °C lasting 0.1 s stores P0DF7-00. The circuit itself is electrically fine in this case, so wiring checks rarely help, and Mitsubishi's procedure replaces the power drive unit. A genuine overheat of the inverter is reported separately as P0A3E. The same comparison on sensor B is P0DF4.

causes.label: Sensor C drifted or stuck inside the IGBT module
Internal fault of the power drive unit
Control software misjudging the comparison

symptoms: Engine warning light on after a cold start
Usually no noticeable change in driving
Possibly reduced generator power

P0DF8.title: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor C Circuit Low
P0DF8.description: P0DF8 tells that temperature sensor C in the generator inverter delivers a voltage below its valid range. Mitsubishi uses the code in the Outlander PHEV for the W-phase high-side IGBT sensor: a reading at or under 1.25 V for 0.08 s, with at least 8 V GCU supply, stores P0DF8-00, and the check runs all the time. Physical causes are a short between signal and ground or a breakdown inside the module, for instance after coolant has reached the electronics. The value suggests a far too hot switch, so the controller derates the generator to stay on the safe side. The sensor cannot be replaced on its own, which is why Mitsubishi lists the power drive unit. The same fault on sensor B is P0DF5, the high case on this sensor P0DF9.

causes.label: Signal line of sensor C shorted to ground
Coolant or moisture inside the inverter electronics
Shorted sensor or internal fault of the power drive unit

symptoms: Hybrid or engine warning light on
Generator power limited
Implausibly high inverter temperature in live data

P0DF9.title: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor C Circuit High
P0DF9.description: P0DF9 is stored when the C temperature sensor of the generator inverter reports a voltage at or beyond the upper end of its window. For the Outlander PHEV Mitsubishi defines the limit as 3.75 V for 0.08 s on the W-phase high-side IGBT sensor, monitored continuously whenever the GCU has at least 8 V. An open line, a backed-out terminal in the inverter connector or a broken sensor element are the usual explanations. Unlike a real cold start, the reading does not climb as the generator works, which separates the fault from a true low temperature. Generator power may be held back until the value is valid again, and Mitsubishi fixes it by replacing the complete power drive unit. Too low a voltage on the same sensor is P0DF8; the B-sensor counterpart is P0DF6.

causes.label: Open signal line of sensor C
Terminal pushed back in the inverter connector
Broken sensor element inside the power drive unit

symptoms: Engine or hybrid warning light on
Inverter temperature stuck at a very low value
Generator output held back

P0DFA.title: Generator Phase U-V-W Current Sensor Correlation
P0DFA.description: In a three-phase machine the currents of phases U, V and W add up to nearly zero at every instant, so a sum far from zero shows that at least one current sensor is wrong. P0DFA is the code for this cross-check on the generator side. Mitsubishi documents it for the Outlander PHEV: with the IGBTs switching, the summation check must not report a failure, and with them off the sum must stay below 140 A; either condition held for 0.35 s sets P0DFA-00. Ford counts P0DFA among the generator inverter faults of its power-split hybrids, and SSM 50151 notes that on 2020 to 2021 hybrid models it can be caused by a 12 V dip at key-on, so check for low voltage first. Single-phase sensor faults are P0E00 to P0E0B.

causes.label: 12 V voltage drop at key-on (Ford SSM 50151)
One phase current sensor with offset or gain error
Internal fault of the inverter or power drive unit

symptoms: Stop Safely Now or hybrid system warning
Vehicle may not start or ready mode is refused
Generator shut down, restricted driving

P0DFB.title: Generator Position Exceeding Learn Limit
P0DFB.description: The position sensor of a hybrid generator, normally a resolver, is never mounted exactly in line with the magnetic poles of the rotor. The remaining angle error is determined once and saved in the controller; Hyundai describes doing this after assembly and again whenever the machine or its control unit is replaced, and Ford describes an in-vehicle routine started by a scan tool that sweeps the current angle and reads the offset where the q-axis current crosses zero. P0DFB means such a learned offset lies outside the window the software accepts, so it cannot be used for field-oriented control. No manufacturer documents P0DFB publicly. Possible reasons are a resolver that moved on its shaft, an aborted learning run or a faulty controller. A missing value is P0DFC instead.

causes.label: Offset learning interrupted or run under wrong conditions
Resolver rotor or stator shifted after repair or damage
Fault or wrong software in the generator control unit

symptoms: Hybrid system warning and engine warning light
Generator not used, reduced charging or engine start problems
Code returns after clearing until relearned

P0DFC.title: Generator Position Sensor Not Learned
P0DFC.description: P0DFC is stored when the controller has no valid learned position offset for the generator resolver. Ford explains it in the OBD summary of its power-split hybrids: the code appears when the resolver was not configured at the assembly plant or after the inverter system controller has been replaced, and the check fails if the value held in EEPROM is outside its accepted range. It runs continuously from 700 ms after power-up with 6 to 19 V on the 12 V system, and Ford's 2014 code list marks P0DFC as a MIL code. Volvo reported intermittent IGM-P0DFC00 entries without symptoms on 2016 to 2017 XC90 T8 models and later released new IGM software. After a module or generator replacement, run the learn procedure. The drive motor counterpart is P0C17.

causes.label: Inverter or hybrid controller replaced without resolver learning
Software fault in the inverter generator module (Volvo, update available)
Stored offset lost or corrupted in EEPROM

symptoms: Engine warning light on
Generator or hybrid functions restricted
Sometimes only stored as history code without symptoms

P0DFD.title: Battery Charger Coolant Control Valve Control Circuit/Open
P0DFD.description: P0DFD flags an open or otherwise faulty drive circuit of the valve that controls coolant flow through the on-board charger. Such a valve lets the thermal system send coolant to the charger during AC charging and bypass it while driving. No manufacturer documents P0DFD publicly. The nearest documented case is the coolant shutoff valve of the battery module in Mercedes S-, E- and C-Class hybrids, whose actuation fault or open circuit the battery management logs as P0CDF00 (LI83.30-P-061224). CARB names thermal management of the battery and of the inverter explicitly, not the charger, so whether the MIL lights is up to the maker. A charger that runs too hot will cut its power, so charging may become slower. Shorts are P0DFE and P0DFF.

causes.label: Broken wire or unplugged connector at the valve
Open coil or motor winding in the valve
Faulty output stage in the controlling module

symptoms: Charging slower than usual or interrupted
Charging or service message
Driving usually unaffected

P0DFE.title: Battery Charger Coolant Control Valve Control Circuit Low
P0DFE.description: P0DFE means the control line of the charger coolant valve reads low, usually because it is shorted to ground somewhere between driver and valve. No manufacturer documents P0DFE publicly. GM's 2011 Volt tables show how such a check works on battery coolant valve A (P0CE2): with system voltage above 9 V and the valve commanded in reverse, a low sense level on drive 1 counts as a failure, and the code needs a fault in 90 of 100 checks spaced 6.25 ms apart before it is set as a two-trip Type B code. For the charger valve a similar logic is likely but not published. A ground short typically freezes the valve where it is, so the charger may be left without coolant and lower its power. Look for chafed wires and wet connectors. Open circuit is P0DFD.

causes.label: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Coolant or water in the valve connector
Internal short in the valve actuator

symptoms: Reduced charging power, longer charging time
Charger warning or charging stops
Driving normally unaffected

P0DFF.title: Battery Charger Coolant Control Valve Control Circuit High
P0DFF.description: P0DFF is the short-to-voltage case for the valve that cools the on-board charger. The controller sees the drive line high while commanding it low. No manufacturer documents P0DFF publicly. The closest published logic is GM's 2011 Volt monitor for battery coolant valve A (P0CE3). It watches for a high sense level on drive 1 while the valve is stopped or moving forward, above 9 V system voltage, and stores a two-trip Type B code only after 90 bad results in 100 samples taken at 6.25 ms intervals. If the wire is stuck at battery potential the actuator stays powered, and the valve can travel to its end position rather than stopping where it was. If that leaves the charger uncooled, charging power drops. Usual causes are chafed insulation touching a powered conductor or an output stage that fails to turn off. Ground short is P0DFE.

causes.label: Control wire shorted to a supply voltage
Output stage in the controlling module will not switch off
Internal fault in the valve actuator

symptoms: Charging slower or charger warning
Valve audibly running to its end stop
Driving normally unaffected
